findings.title: Unreachable true-branch in SCENARIO_EXPANDER outputs merge (`if outputs is None`)
findings.description: In `overlay_declared_contract`, the SCENARIO_EXPANDER output-merge guard is entered only when `builder.outputs is not None`. By that point `outputs` was assigned `declared.outputs if declared.outputs is not None else builder.outputs`, so when `builder.outputs is not None` the else-branch already guarantees `outputs is not None` (it falls back to the non-None `builder.outputs`). Therefore inside the guard `outputs is None` can never be true, making the ternary's consequent `builder.outputs` dead. The expression only ever evaluates the else-branch `outputs | builder.outputs`. The branch is a behavior-preserving no-op that can be simplified to `outputs = outputs | builder.outputs`.
findings.evidence:
Line 596-599:
  inputs = declared.inputs if declared.inputs is not None else builder.inputs  # (596)
  outputs = declared.outputs if declared.outputs is not None else builder.outputs  # (597)
  if node.data.nodeType == NodeType.SCENARIO_EXPANDER and builder.outputs is not None:  # (598)
      outputs = builder.outputs if outputs is None else outputs | builder.outputs  # (599)
Trace: entering 598 requires builder.outputs is not None. Two cases for `outputs` from line 597: (a) declared.outputs is not None -> outputs = declared.outputs (a frozenset, not None); (b) declared.outputs is None -> outputs = builder.outputs which is not None here. In both cases `outputs is None` is False, so the `builder.outputs` consequent at line 599 is unreachable. (The early-return path in `_empty_declared_contract_should_defer_to_builder` (614-615) handles the empty-declared SCENARIO_EXPANDER case before line 598 is reached, so it cannot make `outputs` None either.)
findings.est_reduction: ~1 line / one dead conditional arm; replace ternary with `outputs = outputs | builder.outputs`.
findings.behavior_preservation: The dead consequent is `builder.outputs`; the live arm is `outputs | builder.outputs`. Since `outputs is None` is provably never true inside the guard, the observable result is unchanged for all inputs. Removing the unreachable arm preserves behavior exactly.

coverage.notes: Examined all 31 in-scope functions in full (lines 1-836) plus required cross-file definitions (Contract.from_user_declared/from_tuple/to_tuple in _contracts.py; _has_user_polars_code, _has_projection_user_code, SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule, declared_inputs_by_parent, _literal_string in projection.py) to judge correctness. Several candidate issues were investigated and dismissed as non-bugs because they are either caller-guaranteed invariants or intentional, test-backed design decisions: (1) source_scan_projection demanding a physical column for a renamed-away/duplicate logical output is unreachable given the planner only seeds valid output names (and polars rejects duplicate outputs at execution); (2) source_user_code_preserves_column_projection returning False for pure-passthrough code with no df assignment is a conservative (correctness-safe) full-width fallback, consistent with the module's no-guessing philosophy; (3) overlay_declared_contract treating a declared `contract: "opaque"` as deferring to a concrete builder contract is INTENTIONAL and explicitly asserted by tests/test_execute_lazy_contracts.py::test_effective_contract_declared_opaque_preserves_builder_contract (overlay cannot distinguish field-absent from field-None, by design); (4) overlay_declared_contract dropping declared.inputs_by_parent from its returned Contract is latent-only because fan-in routing re-reads config via declared_inputs_by_parent rather than the overlay result; (5) strict_projection_required's unused required_columns_by_node param is a deliberately-marked (`_ = ...`) stable-API placeholder across 3 call sites, not worth churning. The known-findings list (compute_prepared_plan seed drop, PolarsFanInRule passthrough inference, _format_contract_source ownership guess, SIMP-3) all concern code outside this line range and were not re-reported.

findings.location: src/haute/projection.py:1212-1218 (_unordered_expression_demands, filter branch); contrast the correct ordered branch at :1118-1126; manifests through SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule.parent_demands (:1277-1299)
findings.title: Unordered demand walk omits filter keyword-constraint columns, under-demanding the parent for df.filter(col='value')
findings.description: In _unordered_expression_demands the `filter` branch only collects columns via _referenced_polars_columns(ast_node), which recognises pl.col(...) references. It never accounts for Polars keyword-constraint filters such as df.filter(segment='A'), where the keyword name `segment` IS a required column (df.filter(seg='A') is sugar for df.filter(pl.col('seg')=='A')). The ordered branch already handles this exact case (line 1125 adds `{kw.arg for kw in call.keywords if kw.arg is not None}` with the comment "Keyword constraints (df.filter(segment='A')) name columns"), so the two demand walks are inconsistent. Code containing only df.filter(segment='A') has no rename/select/derived-reference, so _single_parent_polars_expression_demands routes it straight to the unordered walk (not the ordered one), returning a parent demand that omits `segment`. compute_prepared_plan writes routed_demands.by_parent verbatim into edge_demands (projection.py:2253-2256), so the parent scan is narrowed to exclude `segment`; the filter then fails at execution with ColumnNotFoundError on otherwise-valid user code (or, if the column is genuinely present upstream and pruned, the filter loses a required input). This breaks a very common single-parent feature-engineering shape.
findings.evidence: Verified at the in-scope rule contract. SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule().parent_demands(node='df = df.filter(segment=\'A\')', parent_ids=['p1'], my_needed={'premium'}) returns by_parent={'p1': {'premium'}} -- 'segment' is MISSING. The ordered extractor for the same code returns {'premium','segment'} (correct). Polars confirms the column is required: df.filter(segment='A') on a frame lacking 'segment' raises ColumnNotFoundError("unable to find column 'segment'"). Root cause: _unordered_expression_demands filter branch (1212-1218) never reads call.keywords, whereas the ordered branch (1118-1126) does. Mixed shapes are equally affected: 'df = df.with_columns((pl.col(\'x\')+1).alias(\'y\'))\ndf = df.filter(seg=\'B\')' with needed={y} returns {'x'} (drops 'seg') because the derived-reference router does not detect a keyword-named column and the unordered walk drops it.

findings.location: src/haute/projection.py:789-802 (_referenced_polars_columns) used by in-scope _select_output_to_input (:845-847), _unordered_expression_demands (:1204,1213) and _ordered_expression_demands via _call_argument_columns; manifests through SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule.parent_demands
findings.title: String-argument Polars aggregation shortcuts (pl.sum('a'), pl.mean('a'), ...) contribute zero column references, silently under-demanding the parent
findings.description: _referenced_polars_columns only treats pl.col('name') as a column reference and returns None (forcing the safe full-width boundary) ONLY for a dynamic/unknown `.col(...)`. Polars top-level aggregation shortcuts that name a column by string argument -- pl.sum('a'), pl.mean('a'), pl.min/max/first/last/std/var/median/count/n_unique('a') -- are NOT pl.col calls, so _referenced_polars_columns silently returns an empty set for them instead of bailing. This contradicts the module's stated design (bail to full width on anything unprovable). Several of these are row-preserving when used inside with_columns (e.g. df.with_columns(pl.sum('a').alias('s')) broadcasts the column sum across all rows and is a valid single-parent shape), so they legitimately reach the demand walks. The with_columns ordered guard at line 1145 does NOT bail because the expression is aliased (_alias_name is not None). The result is a parent demand that omits the referenced column; the narrowed parent scan then fails at execution with ColumnNotFoundError on valid user code. Unlike finding 1 this affects BOTH the ordered and unordered walks (and _select_output_to_input), because they share _referenced_polars_columns.
findings.evidence: Rule-level: SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule().parent_demands(node='df = df.with_columns(pl.sum(\'a\').alias(\'s\'))', parent_ids=['p1'], my_needed={'s'}) returns by_parent={'p1': set()} -- 'a' MISSING. _select_output_to_input(parse('df.select(pl.sum(\'a\').alias(\'s\'))')) yields {'s': set()} (should be {'s': {'a'}}). Polars confirms requirement: df.with_columns(pl.sum('a').alias('s')) on a frame lacking 'a' raises ColumnNotFoundError. By contrast the pl.col form df.select(pl.col('a').sum().alias('s')) is captured correctly (returns {'a'}), showing the gap is specifically the string-argument shortcut functions. Safe alternative would be to return None from _referenced_polars_columns (or bail in the branch) when a pl.<func>(<string>) expression cannot be proven column-free, matching the existing dynamic-pl.col() bail at lines 796-801.

findings.location: src/haute/projection.py:1396-1403 (_raise_if_unbounded_user_code_is_terminal); sole call site at :2268-2273 in compute_prepared_plan

findings.title: _raise_if_unbounded_user_code_is_terminal is a no-op whose name promises a guard it never performs
findings.description: _raise_if_unbounded_user_code_is_terminal accepts (node, parent_ids, *, strict_projection) and its entire body is `_ = node, parent_ids, strict_projection` followed by `return`. It never raises and never inspects anything. It is called once, in compute_prepared_plan's `if my_needed is None:` branch, immediately before unconditionally writing an opaque ParentDemandResult. The name strongly implies a loud guard (consistent with the project's fail-loudly philosophy) that does not exist, which is misleading to readers and a maintenance trap. It appears to be leftover scaffolding (introduced in commit 33b41036 'backend hardening and optimisation'). Either it should be implemented to actually raise when terminal unbounded user code would silently widen, or both the no-op and its call site should be deleted.

findings.title: _freeze_plan rebuilds dict(node_reasons) once per opaque boundary inside the comprehension
findings.description: In _freeze_plan the opaque_reasons MappingProxyType is built with a dict comprehension `{node_id: dict(node_reasons or {}).get(node_id, <default>) for node_id in opaque_boundaries}`. The expression `dict(node_reasons or {})` is re-evaluated on EVERY iteration, materialising a fresh copy of the entire node_reasons mapping for each opaque boundary. With O(n) opaque boundaries and an O(m) node_reasons map this is O(n*m) allocation/copy work to perform what is logically n lookups. node_reasons is already a Mapping (Mapping[str, ProjectionReason] | None), so `(node_reasons or {}).get(node_id, default)` performs the identical lookup with zero copies, and the surrounding code already separately builds the canonical copy once at line 2390 (node_reasons=MappingProxyType(dict(node_reasons or {}))). The per-iteration default ProjectionReason(rule='opaque_demand', message='opaque demand') is likewise reconstructed each iteration but could be hoisted to a module constant since ProjectionReason is frozen.
findings.evidence: Line 2380: `node_id: dict(node_reasons or {}).get(node_id, ProjectionReason(...))` sits inside `for node_id in opaque_boundaries` (line 2387). dict(...) copies the whole mapping per node_id. node_reasons is typed Mapping (param annotation line 2367), so .get works without the dict() wrapper; the same value is copied again standalone at line 2390. No mutation of node_reasons occurs between, so the repeated copy is pure waste.
findings.est_reduction: ~2-3 lines net plus removing O(n*m) copies; replace with a single hoisted `reasons = node_reasons or {}` (and a module-level default ProjectionReason) used inside the comprehension.
findings.behavior_preservation: Identical output: dict(M).get(k, d) and M.get(k, d) return the same value for any Mapping M; node_reasons is not mutated during the comprehension, so hoisting the copy out (or dropping it entirely in favour of the original Mapping) is byte-for-byte behaviour-preserving. The default ProjectionReason is frozen/immutable so sharing one instance is equivalent to constructing fresh ones.

findings.title: join_parent_demands attributes a suffix-stripped column to BOTH join parents, over-demanding the left and risking a spurious loud failure
findings.description: For a simple inferred join with a non-empty suffix, join_parent_demands walks the demanded output_columns and, for every column ending in `join.suffix`, strips the suffix and adds the resulting `parent_column` to BOTH `join.left_parent` and `join.right_parent` (lines 2055-2056). In Polars only the RIGHT operand's colliding column is renamed to `<col><suffix>`; the LEFT operand keeps `<col>` under its original name. Therefore `<col><suffix>` is owned solely by the right parent, and demanding `<col>` from the left parent is an over-demand. In the common case the left parent physically has `<col>` (that is exactly why the collision/suffix arose), so this only widens the left scan harmlessly. But when the left parent does NOT physically produce `<col>` (e.g. the suffixed name collides with a right-only column whose base name the left lacks), the edge projection guard in _execute_lazy._apply_edge_projection (`missing = demand - schema_set`, raises ContractMismatchError) turns a perfectly valid join into a loud 'columns missing from the parent frame' failure. The mis-attribution to the left is provably present; it is over-demand (never a silent mispricing) but can convert a valid graph into a spurious hard error. This is distinct from the known passthrough-parent misroute (catalog #57 / known item 2), which concerns simple_left_join_passthrough_parent / unambiguous_passthrough_parent routing UN-suffixed collision columns; here the defect is in the SUFFIXED-column branch of join_parent_demands which neither of those known items touches.
findings.evidence: Lines 2049-2057: `for column in output_columns - handled: if not column.endswith(join.suffix): continue; parent_column = column[:-len(join.suffix)]; ...; demands.setdefault(join.left_parent, set()).add(parent_column); demands.setdefault(join.right_parent, set()).add(parent_column)`. Both left and right get parent_column. join_parent_demands has exactly one caller: PolarsFanInRule.parent_demands (line 1482) for the uncovered `missing` set under a declared inputs_by_parent contract; its result is OR'd into by_parent (lines 1488-1491) and then validated per-parent against the parent's PHYSICAL schema by _apply_edge_projection (_execute_lazy.py:1044-1056), which raises ContractMismatchError when demand - schema_set is non-empty. Polars suffix semantics (confirmed in catalog #57's ground-truth check): the right copy becomes `<col><suffix>`, the left keeps `<col>`.

findings.title: Expression renderer drops required parentheses around Compare/BoolOp/IfExp/UnaryOp operands and around equal-precedence right-Pow, so the human-readable formula re-parses to a DIFFERENT value
findings.description: _binop only adds parentheses when a child is itself an ast.BinOp (lines 223 and 225 both guard on `isinstance(node.left/right, ast.BinOp)`), and uses strict `<` precedence. This produces formulas that, when read by a human or re-parsed, compute a different number than the original Polars expression. Confirmed manifestations: (1) Compare operand inside arithmetic: `(pl.col('a') > pl.col('b')) + 1` renders as `a > b + 1`, which re-parses as `a > (b + 1)` (a boolean vs an arithmetic compare). (2) Unary-minus as power base: `(-pl.col('a')) ** 2` renders as `-a ** 2`, which Python parses as `-(a**2)` (sign flips for even powers). (3) Right-associative `**`: `(pl.col('a') ** pl.col('b')) ** pl.col('c')` renders as `a ** b ** c`, which re-parses as `a ** (b ** c)` (because the left-paren rule uses `<`, not `<=`, for the right-associative Pow). (4) IfExp operand: `(a if c else b) + 1` renders as `a if c else b + 1` -> reparses as `a if c else (b + 1)`. (5) BoolOp precedence in _boolop: `(a or b) and c` renders as `a or b and c`, which reparses as `a or (b and c)` because _boolop never wraps a lower-precedence `or` child inside an `and`. The rendered `expression_text` (and the parallel substituted_text) is written into user-facing trace lineage (`step.calculation`/`source_info`, per catalog finding 38), so the actuary is shown a formula that does not match the actual computation. This is the project's explicit fail-loud-vs-silent-wrong concern: a confidently-wrong formula with no error.
findings.evidence: Ran the real _ExprConverter: `(a > b) + 1` -> 'a > b + 1'; `(-a) ** 2` -> '-a ** 2'; `(a ** b) ** c` -> 'a ** b ** c'; `(a if c else b) + 1` -> 'a if c else b + 1'; `(a or b) and c` -> 'a or b and c'. Each rendered string re-parses with different operator grouping than the source. Root cause: _binop paren guards at lines 223/225 test only `isinstance(..., ast.BinOp)` so Compare/UnaryOp/IfExp/BoolOp children are never parenthesized; and line 223 uses `_op_prec(node.left.op) < _op_prec(node.op)` (strict `<`) which omits parens for an equal-precedence left Pow that right-associativity actually requires. _boolop (257-260) joins values with no precedence awareness. Existing tests (test_expression_parser.py:189-207) only pin `+/-/*` precedence; none cover Compare-in-BinOp, unary-in-Pow, Pow associativity, IfExp-in-BinOp, or and/or mixing, so these slipped through.

findings.title: _name recurses into symbol-table entries with no visited-guard, so a self-/mutually-referential top-level assignment causes RecursionError (masked to a silently-opaque expression)
findings.description: _name resolves a variable by recursively calling self.convert(self._symbol_table[name]) (lines 280-283) with no cycle/visited tracking. The feeding symbol tables (_build_safe_symbol_table:792-808 and _build_symbol_table:776-789) capture any top-level `name = <non-df-expr>` assignment, including self-referential ones like `factor = factor * 2` and mutually-referential pairs like `a = b + 1; b = a + 1`. When such a variable is used in the with_columns target expression, _name -> convert(BinOp) -> _binop -> convert(Name) -> _name loops until Python's recursion limit, raising RecursionError. parse_expression's broad `except Exception` (988-1003) then swallows it and returns an `expression_type='opaque'` result with no columns/constants/formula. Net effect: an otherwise-parseable expression is silently downgraded to opaque (all lineage lost) after burning a full deep recursion stack, instead of being resolved or cleanly skipped. This is distinct from the catalogued catch-all finding (which documents that the catch-all masks failures); here the specific defect is the unbounded recursion inside in-scope _name, which has no business looping.
findings.evidence:
End-to-end via the real public entry: parse_expression('factor = factor * 2
df = df.with_columns(factor.alias("out"))', 'out') returns expression_type='opaque', referenced_columns=[] (the formula `factor * 2` and the column are lost). Mutual case ('a = b + 1
b = a + 1
...with_columns(a.alias("out"))') likewise -> opaque. Direct converter call on a symtab {'x': <BinOp x+1>} converting Name('x') raises RecursionError. _build_safe_symbol_table:797-803 confirms `x = x + 1` is captured (ast.Assign, Name target, RHS BinOp is not a df-assignment). RecursionError subclasses Exception, so the parse-boundary catch-all converts the crash into the opaque sentinel.

findings.title: f-string format specs and conversions (:fmt, !r/!s/!a) are silently dropped — wrong RESOLVED ALIAS (column name) via _try_eval_fstring, and lossy formula text via _joinedstr
findings.description: Both f-string handlers ignore FormattedValue.format_spec and FormattedValue.conversion. In _joinedstr a FormattedValue is rendered as `{<value>}` (line 334), dropping any `:.2f`/`!r`. More seriously, _try_eval_fstring (used by _strip_alias to statically evaluate an f-string ALIAS into the target column name) folds a FormattedValue by appending only str(resolved-constant) (lines 736-747), ignoring the format spec. So an alias `pl.col('a').alias(f"col_{idx:02d}")` with idx=3 resolves to 'col_3' instead of the actual Polars output column name 'col_03'. The parser then attributes the expression to the wrong column name, so target-column matching/lineage is mis-labelled (a correctness defect, not merely display).
findings.evidence: Real _strip_alias on `pl.col('a').alias(f"col_{idx:02d}")` with symbol table {'idx': Constant(3)} returns alias='col_3'; Python's f'col_{3:02d}' is 'col_03' -> mismatch. Real _ExprConverter on `f"{x:.2f}"` -> 'f"{x}"' and on `f"{x!r}"` -> 'f"{x}"' (spec/conversion dropped). _try_eval_fstring lines 736-745 only branch on ast.Name (symtab Constant) and ast.Constant and never inspect v.format_spec / v.conversion.

findings.location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:300-303 (_subscript) — missing ast.Slice handler in convert (152-186)
findings.title: Sliced subscripts render as raw ast.dump garbage (e.g. 'a[Slice(lower=Constant(value=1), upper=Constant(value=2))]') because convert has no ast.Slice case
findings.description: _subscript renders the slice via self.convert(node.slice). For a plain index `a[0]` node.slice is a Constant (handled), but for a slice `a[1:2]` node.slice is an ast.Slice, which convert (152-186) does not dispatch on — it falls through to the `return ast.dump(node)` fallback (line 186). The resulting human-readable text contains a raw AST repr ('Slice(lower=Constant(value=1), upper=Constant(value=2))') instead of '1:2'. Polars expressions can produce subscript-with-slice (e.g. Expr.__getitem__ slicing or struct/array indexing), so this leaks internal AST text into the user-facing formula.
findings.evidence: Real _ExprConverter on `a[1:2]` returns 'a[Slice(lower=Constant(value=1), upper=Constant(value=2))]'. convert() (152-186) lists handlers for BinOp/UnaryOp/Compare/BoolOp/Call/Constant/Name/Attribute/Subscript/List/Tuple/Dict/IfExp/JoinedStr/Starred/Expr but not Slice, so node.slice of type ast.Slice hits ast.dump at line 186.

findings.title: _constant does not escape embedded double-quotes, producing malformed/ambiguous formula text
findings.description: _constant renders a str literal as f'"{val}"' (line 271) without escaping any `"` characters inside val. A column/string compared against a value containing a double quote (e.g. `pl.col('a') == 'he said "hi"'`) renders as `a == "he said "hi""`, which is not valid/round-trippable text and is ambiguous to a human reader. The same unescaped pattern is repeated in _pl_lit (line 494). Lower severity (display fidelity), but it is the formula surfaced to actuaries and breaks any consumer that re-parses the text.
findings.evidence: Real _ExprConverter on `pl.col('a') == 'he said "hi"'` returns 'a == "he said "hi""' (the inner quotes are emitted verbatim, closing the string early on re-parse). Source line 271 `return f'"{val}"'` performs no escaping; repr(val) (which would escape) is used only for the non-str int/float/other branches.

findings.title: ast.walk BFS ordering breaks 'last match wins' for chained .with_columns(...).with_columns(...) that redefine the same column, selecting the shadowed (overwritten) definition
findings.description: _find_with_columns_calls collects with_columns/select calls via ast.walk(tree). ast.walk is breadth-first, so for a single chained expression df.with_columns(A).with_columns(B) the OUTER call (B, which Polars applies LAST and which therefore wins) is yielded BEFORE the inner call (A). parse_expression (and _compute_result_impl and _evaluate_conditional_branches) iterate wc_calls and keep the LAST alias match ('last match wins', comment at line 1078). Because walk order is reverse-of-execution for chained calls, the loop's 'last' is actually the inner/earliest (shadowed) definition A, not the effective definition B. The displayed formula, expression_type, referenced_columns AND the computed result_value all reflect the overwritten definition. No exception is raised, so the broad except-catch-all (known finding #23) is NOT involved — this is a confidently-wrong value/formula. Note the equivalent code written as two SEPARATE statements works correctly, because there the two Assign/Call nodes are siblings at the same depth and ast.walk preserves their source order; only the chained form is wrong.
findings.evidence: Executed repro (uv run, Polars 1.39.2) on the real public API. code = 'df = df.with_columns((pl.col("a") + 1).alias("out")).with_columns((pl.col("a") + 100).alias("out"))'. _find_with_columns_calls walk order prints the +100 call FIRST then the +1 call. parse_expression(code,'out').expression_text == 'a + 1' (WRONG; Polars effective is a+100). evaluate_expression(code,'out',{'a':10}).result_value == 11 and substituted_text == '10 + 1' (WRONG; Polars truth = 110). Control: the same logic as two separate statements yields expression_text=='a + 100' and result_value==110 (correct), isolating the chained form + ast.walk ordering as the cause.

findings.location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1171-1181 (_expr_references_vars), reached from _parse_expression_impl:1138-1147; interacts with _find_control_flow_assigned_vars:843-851 and _build_safe_symbol_table:792-808
findings.title: _expr_references_vars's 'and child.id not in symbol_table' guard defeats the opaque bailout when a control-flow-reassigned variable also has a top-level binding, silently dropping the conditional reassignment
findings.description: _parse_expression_impl uses cf_assigned = _find_control_flow_assigned_vars(stmts) and, if the matched expression references any of those vars, returns an opaque ParsedExpression (the intent: an expression depending on a conditionally-assigned variable is not statically resolvable — comment lines 1057-1058). But _expr_references_vars only returns True when a referenced name is in var_names AND 'child.id not in symbol_table'. When the SAME variable is assigned both at top level and reassigned inside an if/for/try (e.g. `factor = pl.col("base")` then `if region=="north": factor = pl.col("base") * 2`), the name is present in symbol_table (from the top-level assignment), so _expr_references_vars returns False, the code is NOT marked opaque, and the variable is resolved to its TOP-LEVEL value only — the conditional reassignment is silently discarded. The parser therefore emits a confidently-wrong formula/result that omits the branch logic, rather than the correct opaque fallback.
findings.evidence: Executed repro: with the top-level binding present, _build_safe_symbol_table -> {'factor'}, _find_control_flow_assigned_vars -> {'factor'}, 'factor' in symbol_table == True, and _expr_references_vars(Name('factor'), {'factor'}, st) == False. parse_expression(code,'out').expression_text == 'base' (type 'arithmetic', refs ['base']) — the `*2` conditional branch is dropped. Contrast: identical code WITHOUT the top-level `factor = pl.col("base")` line yields _expr_references_vars == True and parse_expression(...).expression_type == 'opaque' (correct). This isolates the 'also has a top-level binding' case as the trigger and shows the guard clause `and child.id not in symbol_table` is the defect.

findings.title: _substitute_values corrupts an already-substituted string value when a later (shorter) column name matches a word inside the inserted string literal
findings.description: _substitute_values replaces column names in expression_text one at a time, sorted by name length descending (to avoid prefix collisions). _format_value renders a string column value as a quoted literal (e.g. '"base rate"'). The length-sort only protects against one column name being a prefix of another; it does NOT protect already-inserted VALUES. After substituting a string-valued column, the inserted literal can contain a token equal to another (later-processed) column name; _replace_column_name then matches that token (via \bname\b word boundaries, where spaces are word boundaries) inside the quoted string and overwrites it, producing a corrupted user-facing 'calculation' text. The substituted_text is surfaced to the actuary as the computed calculation (written into step.calculation/source_info by _trace_enrichment), so the displayed formula is demonstrably wrong even though result_value is computed independently.
findings.evidence: Executed end-to-end via the public evaluate_expression: code='df = df.with_columns(pl.concat_str([pl.col("label"), pl.col("rate")]).alias("out"))', row={'label':'base rate','rate':5}. expression_text='concat_str(label, rate)', input_values={'label':'base rate','rate':5}, but substituted_text='concat_str("base 5", 5)' — the literal "base rate" was mangled to "base 5" because column name 'rate' matched the word 'rate' inside the already-substituted string. findings.title: Outer .otherwise() containing a nested when corrupts outer branch metadata (reports wrong taken_branch/index/dimmed)
findings.description: In _BranchTrackingEvaluator._eval_clauses, the `then` path sets `self._is_outer = False` (line 2094) before recursing into the then value, but the `otherwise` path (lines 2107-2113) sets taken_branch/taken_branch_index/dimmed_branches WITHOUT clearing `self._is_outer`. So when the outer `.otherwise()` value itself contains a nested when-chain, `self.evaluate(clause['otherwise'])` (line 2113) recurses into the inner chain's _eval_clauses with `is_outer = self._is_outer` still True. The inner chain then overwrites taken_branch/taken_branch_index/dimmed_branches with ITS OWN (inner) values, clobbering the outer's. The trace therefore reports that the outer THEN clause fired when in fact the outer OTHERWISE fired. This metadata is serialized verbatim into step.calculation via dataclasses.asdict(evaluated) (_trace_enrichment.py:1523) and drives which clause the explainability UI highlights/dims, so the user is shown the wrong branch as taken.
findings.evidence: Executed repro (polars 1.39.2). Code: out=pl.when(pl.col('a')>0).then(99).otherwise(pl.when(pl.col('b')>0).then(1).otherwise(2)); row a=-1,b=1. _compute_result_impl returns 1 (correct: outer-otherwise -> inner-then). But _evaluate_conditional_branches returns {'taken_branch':'then','taken_branch_index':0,'dimmed_branches':[1],'nested_branches':[]} — claiming the outer THEN (value 99, index 0) was taken, which is false; the outer OTHERWISE (index 1) fired. Root cause: otherwise branch lacks the `self._is_outer = False` that the then branch has at line 2094, so the nested evaluate() overwrites the just-set outer metadata.

findings.title: nested_branches always records "then" for a nested conditional, regardless of which inner branch actually fired
findings.description: When the taken outer `.then()` contains a nested when-chain, lines 2098-2100 append `self.taken_branch` to `nested_branches` intending to capture the inner branch that fired. But `self._is_outer` was set False at line 2094 BEFORE `self.evaluate(then_node)` runs at line 2096, so the nested _eval_clauses invocation sees `is_outer=False` and never updates `self.taken_branch`. At line 2100 `self.taken_branch` is therefore still the outer's "then", and `self.taken_branch or 'then'` always appends "then". The inner-otherwise case is thus mislabelled as inner-then. nested_branches is surfaced to the trace UI (EvaluatedExpression.nested_branches -> dataclasses.asdict). The intended semantics (record the inner branch kind) are never achievable with the current ordering.
findings.evidence: Executed repro. Code: out=pl.when(pl.col('a')>0).then(pl.when(pl.col('b')>0).then(1).otherwise(2)).otherwise(3). With a=1,b=-1 the inner OTHERWISE fires (result_value=2, confirmed via _compute_result_impl), yet _evaluate_conditional_branches returns nested_branches=['then'] (expected ['otherwise']). With a=1,b=1 (inner then) it also returns ['then'] — so the field is constant 'then' whenever a nested-in-then conditional is taken, carrying no real information. Additionally, a nested when inside the OTHERWISE branch is never recorded in nested_branches at all (the append only exists in the cond/then path), confirmed: a=-1,b=1 gives nested_branches=[].

findings.title: Unary ~ (Invert) does Python bitwise-not on booleans instead of Polars logical-not (~True shown as -2)
findings.description: _unaryop maps ast.Invert to `return ~val`. For boolean inputs this is Python bitwise complement: `~True == -2`, `~False == -1`. But in Polars `~pl.col('mask')` on a Boolean column is LOGICAL negation (`~True -> False`, `~False -> True`), and `~pl.col('flag')` is one of the most common Polars idioms for negating a predicate/mask. The evaluator therefore displays a meaningless signed integer (-1/-2) as the computed value for a negated boolean in the trace waterfall, instead of the boolean Polars actually produces. This null/bool divergence is not one of the broad categories the catalog enumerates (the replace finding lists null-propagation / branch-selection / string-coercion / aggregation; unary boolean ~ is none of these) and is far more commonly hit than the horizontal-func edge cases already catalogued.
findings.evidence: Executed repro (polars 1.39.2). Code: out=~pl.col('flag'). flag=True -> evaluator result_value=-2, real Polars=False. flag=False -> evaluator=-1, real Polars=True. The AST for ~pl.col('flag') is UnaryOp(op=Invert), routed to line 1647-1648 which returns ~True == -2.

findings.title: _compare silently treats unsupported comparison operators (is/is not/in/not in) as passing, returning True
findings.description: _compare builds cmp_map for Eq/NotEq/Lt/LtE/Gt/GtE only. For any other comparison operator (ast.Is, ast.IsNot, ast.In, ast.NotIn) `fn = cmp_map.get(type(op))` is None, the `if fn:` block is skipped, the loop advances `left = right`, and the function ultimately falls through to `return True`. So an unsupported comparison is silently treated as satisfied rather than failing loudly or returning None. This is a latent correctness hole: any future code path (or a chained comparison mixing a supported and an unsupported op) would silently report True. Reachability through valid Polars expression source is essentially nil (Polars uses .is_in()/.is_null() methods, not Python `in`/`is`), so impact today is low, but the swallow-and-pass behaviour contradicts the project's fail-loud preference and the None-propagation contract used elsewhere in this class.
findings.evidence: Executed repro: _ExprEvaluator({'a':1,'b':2}).evaluate(ast.parse('a is b').body[0].value) -> True (1 is 2 is False); evaluate(ast.parse('a in b').body[0].value) with {'a':9,'b':[1,2,3]} -> True (9 in [1,2,3] is False). The supported chained case 1<5<3 correctly returns False, confirming only the unsupported-op arm is affected.

findings.title: Subclass override of _eval_when_from_then_or_otherwise is byte-identical to the parent and adds nothing
findings.description: _BranchTrackingEvaluator overrides _eval_when_from_then_or_otherwise with a body that is byte-identical to _ExprEvaluator._eval_when_from_then_or_otherwise (both do `clauses = self._collect_eval_clauses(node); return self._eval_clauses(clauses)`). The docstring claims 'Override to track nested branches', but the override changes no behaviour: the branch-tracking happens entirely inside _eval_clauses, which is independently overridden, and Python already dispatches `self._eval_clauses`/`self._collect_eval_clauses` to the subclass via normal MRO. The override can be deleted with zero behavioural change. This is distinct from SIMP-7 (which covers the _eval_when_chain/_eval_chained_when stubs and the _eval_clauses duplication, not this redundant override).
findings.evidence: AST comparison of the two method bodies (docstring stripped) shows identical statement lists: Assign(clauses = self._collect_eval_clauses(node)); Return(self._eval_clauses(clauses)). Equal == True. Removing the subclass method leaves the inherited parent method, which already calls the subclass's overridden _eval_clauses/_collect_eval_clauses, so output is unchanged.
findings.est_reduction: ~4 LOC (one redundant method)
findings.behavior_preservation: Deleting the override leaves the identical inherited implementation, which already dynamically dispatches to the subclass's _eval_clauses and _collect_eval_clauses; no call site or output changes.

findings.title: Falsy `source` is handled three different ways inside _execute_lazy (raw for graph pruning, coerced to "live" for cache-key validation and checkpoint scenario) — latent inconsistency
findings.description: _execute_lazy receives `source: str = "live"`. Graph preparation / live-switch pruning uses the RAW value (`_prepare_graph_with_edges(graph, target_node_id, source=source)` at lines 709-713, which flows into `projection_planner.prune_live_switch_edges` where `source not in input_scenario_map.values()` and `mapped != source` compare against the raw string). However, two other sites in the SAME function silently coerce a falsy source to "live": the dataframe-cache-key source check computes `effective_source = source or "live"` (line 807) and validates `cache_key.source != effective_source`, and the checkpoint-decision scenario passes `node_source_overrides.get(nid, source or "live")` (line 1360). Node builders, meanwhile, receive the raw `source` (via `_build_funcs` `node_source_overrides.get(nid, source)`). If a caller ever passes `source=""` (or any falsy string), the graph would be pruned and node functions built under `""`, while cache admission and checkpoint MODEL_SCORE-skip logic would behave as if `"live"` — three divergent interpretations of one argument. This is a contract inconsistency, not a crash.
findings.evidence: Line 709-713 `_prepare_graph_with_edges(graph, target_node_id, source=source)` → projection.py prune_live_switch_edges compares raw `source`. Line 807 `effective_source = source or "live"` then `if cache_key.source != effective_source: raise`. Line 1360 `_checkpoint_decision(..., node_source_overrides.get(nid, source or "live"))`; _checkpoint_decision (line 440) skips MODEL_SCORE only when `scenario != "live"`. Line 1484 in _build_funcs uses `node_source_overrides.get(nid, source)` (raw). The presence of the defensive `source or "live"` coercion at exactly two of the three sites shows a falsy source was anticipated but not handled uniformly.

findings.title: _enrich_single_table returns matched=True while status='unmatched_value', so a value the trace cannot attribute to any entry or the default is still flagged as a match
findings.description: The returned `matched` field (line 177: `matched and not default_used`, where `matched = rate_value is not None`) is derived purely from value-presence, but `status` (lines 161-168) is derived from `matched_entry is not None`. These diverge for the `unmatched_value` branch: when the rating join produced a NON-null `rate_value` that (a) Python's `normalise_rating_key` walk could not attribute to any `entries` row AND (b) does not equal a usable finite `default_val`, the code sets status='unmatched_value' yet matched=True (and default_used=False). The frontend warning-chip contract relies on `matched`/`default_used` to flag suspicious rows (cf. tests/test_optimiser_apply_trace_enrichment.py:450-451 'frontend warning-chip contract'), so an unattributable value — exactly the suspicious case — is hidden behind matched=True. The single-table convenience path propagates this upward: enrich_rating_step sets result['matched']=t['matched'] (line 248), and the multi-table path ORs t['matched'] (line 256), so the top-level rating detail also reports matched=True for an unmatched_value row. Reachable cases: (1) the documented Float32 non-integer factor-key gap (normalise_rating_key docstring at src/haute/_rating.py:329-333 explicitly excludes non-integer Float32 columns from the engine-agreement guarantee — the engine matches an entry and fills its value, but normalise_rating_key formats the float differently and finds no entry); (2) a non-finite/non-numeric configured defaultValue that the engine nonetheless used (e.g. defaultValue='inf' => default_val=None at lines 132-133 => default_used can never become True at line 155, so a real defaulted miss with a non-null fill becomes status='unmatched_value', matched=True).

Status ladder: not default_used, matched_entry is None, rate_value is not None => line 168 status='unmatched_value'. Return line 177: `matched and not default_used` = True. => {status:'unmatched_value', matched:True, default_used:False}. The existing test test_default_value_infinity (tests/test_trace_enrichment.py:3260) only asserts default_value is None and uses a value (0.5) that isn't the inf fill, so it never checks matched/status for an actually-used non-finite default. findings.title: enrich_steps builds input_frames / source_names / source_ids with DIFFERENT filter predicates, so a missing/None parent output desynchronises the positional alignment and optimiserApply trace selects the wrong parent DataFrame (or raises a spurious index ValueError)
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a (correctness bug, not a simplification)
findings.description: In the optimiserApply branch of enrich_steps the three positionally-correlated argument lists are derived from the same parent_ids list but with non-matching guards: input_frames keeps `pid` only when `pid in eager_outputs and eager_outputs[pid] is not None`, while source_names and source_ids keep `pid` when `pid in node_map`. A parent that failed to execute is ABSENT from eager_outputs (trace.py:768 builds `eager_outputs = {nid: df ... if df is not None}`, so failed/None nodes are dropped) but is still PRESENT in node_map (node_map holds every node). When such a parent precedes a real one, input_frames drops it while source_ids/source_names retain it, so the frames tuple is shorter than / shifted relative to source_ids. The downstream selector _select_optimiser_apply_input (_builders.py:1409-1415) does `index = source_ids.index(ratebook_input); return dfs[index]`, which assumes dfs and source_ids are positionally aligned. Result: in ratebook mode the wrong parent frame is selected, or `index >= len(dfs)` raises the misleading 'expected ratebook_input at index N but received M input(s)' ValueError; in online mode _select_optimiser_apply_input returns `dfs[0]`, so a dropped first parent silently makes dfs[0] the SECOND parent's frame, yielding a confidently-wrong optimiser explanation. The engine's own non-trace build path (_builders.py:1013-1016) deliberately rebuilds dfs in declared-source order to keep dfs/_src_names/_src_ids consistent; the trace path here does not, diverging from that contract. Because the call is wrapped in the per-node try/except, the failure surfaces as a node_detail error marker or a wrong explanation rather than a hard crash.

The `eager_outputs[pid] is not None` guard proves the author anticipated absent/None frames, yet that filter is not applied to source_ids/source_names. _select_optimiser_apply_input (_builders.py:1383-1415) selects `dfs[0]` for online mode and `dfs[source_ids.index(ratebook_input)]` for ratebook mode, both requiring dfs[i] to correspond to source_ids[i]. eager_outputs values are never None / failed nodes are absent (trace.py:768), but node_map contains all nodes (trace.py:_assemble_steps reads node_map[nid] for every ordered node), so a failed/absent parent satisfies `pid in node_map` but not `pid in eager_outputs` — desynchronising the lists. Reachable on the partial-execution trace path (trace.py:514-524 assembles steps for nodes even when the target failed) and whenever an optimiserApply node has ≥1 parent missing from eager_outputs.

findings.title: Banding column contract declares produced output even when the factor has no rules (runtime skips it)
findings.description: _banding_columns reports a factor's outputColumn as a produced column whenever both 'column' and 'outputColumn' are non-empty: `produced = {f["outputColumn"] for f in factors if f.get("outputColumn")}`. But the runtime _apply_banding_factors skips any factor whose rules are empty: `if not col or not out or not rules: continue`. So a banding factor with column+outputColumn set but an empty/absent `rules` list is declared as produced by the contract yet is never created at runtime. The projection demand-propagation subtracts produced columns from upstream demand (projection.py:2321 `base_contribution = (my_needed - produced) | referenced`), so if a downstream node demands that outputColumn, the demand is removed at the banding node (contract claims ownership) but no column is materialised -> downstream select/reference fails with column-not-found in projected/bounded profiles. The contract must apply the same `rules` guard as the executor.
findings.evidence: _banding_columns (l.762) has no rules check; _apply_banding_factors (_rating.py l.244) skips factors with empty rules; projection.py l.2321 subtracts `produced` from upstream demand for concrete contracts (BANDING is concrete, registered via columns=_banding_columns at l.767).

findings.title: Rating-step column contract declares produced output for tables with no factors/entries (runtime skips them)
findings.description: _rating_step_columns adds a table's outputColumn to `produced` for any table with a non-empty outputColumn (l.794-797: `out = t.get("outputColumn", ""); if out: produced.add(out)`), ignoring whether the table has usable `factors`/`entries`. The runtime _apply_rating_table returns the frame unchanged (no column produced) when factors or entries are empty: `if not factors or not entries or not output_col: return lf`. So a rating table with outputColumn set but empty entries (an in-progress config) is declared produced by the contract but never materialised. As with banding, projection.py:2321 subtracts the over-declared `produced` from upstream demand, so a downstream consumer of that outputColumn gets it pruned away yet the runtime never creates it -> column-not-found at materialisation in projected profiles. The contract should mirror the executor's factors/entries guard before declaring a table output as produced.
findings.evidence: _rating_step_columns l.794-797 declares produced from outputColumn presence only; _apply_rating_table (_rating.py l.517) skips tables with empty factors or entries; demand subtraction at projection.py l.2321 applies (RATING_STEP concrete contract via columns=_rating_step_columns at l.807). normalise_rating_tables (_rating_step_config.py l.304) does not drop such tables.

findings.title: scenario_expander step_column contract diverges from runtime when step_column is empty/None
findings.description: The contract reads `sc = config.get("step_column", "scenario_index")` then only adds it to produced if truthy, whereas the builder uses `_step_col = config.get("step_column") or "scenario_index"`. These differ exactly when `step_column` is present but falsy ("" or None): the contract yields `""`/None (falsy) and omits the produced column, while the builder coalesces to "scenario_index" and always produces it. Result: the contract under-declares the produced step-index column for an explicitly-empty step_column. Under-declaring produced means the planner does not treat "scenario_index" as created here; if it happens to exist upstream the demand routing/ownership for it is wrong, and checkpoint projection metadata is inaccurate. Use the same `or` coalescing in the contract (matching the builder) so both agree.
findings.evidence: Contract l.845: `sc = config.get("step_column", "scenario_index")` (default only applies when key absent); builder l.863: `_step_col = config.get("step_column") or "scenario_index"` (default applies for absent, "" and None). Divergence for explicit empty/None step_column.

findings.title: live_switch kwarg path mis-indexes when an upstream frame is absent from dfs_by_name
findings.description: In the kwarg branch, `dfs = tuple(dfs_by_name[name] for name in input_names if name in dfs_by_name)` compacts to only the present names, but the selection loop later indexes the compacted tuple using the position of the matching name within the FULL input_names list: `for i, name in enumerate(input_names): if name == inp: return dfs[i]`. If any earlier input name is missing from dfs_by_name, `i` is offset relative to the compacted `dfs`, so the wrong frame is returned (or IndexError when i >= len(dfs)). The executor itself always calls the function positionally (_execute_lazy.py:1206 `fn(*input_lfs)` and :1856 `result = fn(*input_lfs)`), so this path is only reached by direct kwarg callers (tests/future callers) -- hence the low real-world severity -- but the kwarg contract is silently wrong. The index should be computed against the same filtered name list used to build `dfs`.
findings.evidence: Builder l.645 filters names present in dfs_by_name; l.651-653 indexes dfs by position in unfiltered input_names. Executor passes positional args only (_execute_lazy.py:1206, 1856), so the kwarg branch is exercised solely by direct callers.

findings.title: OUTPUT contract (_passthrough_columns) ignores the fields-based select for non-terminal output nodes
findings.description: output_fn narrows its frame to config['fields'] (`if fields: lf = lf.select(fields)`), but OUTPUT is registered with _passthrough_columns (reads nothing, produces nothing => models full pass-through). The projection layer compensates only when the OUTPUT node is TERMINAL: projection.py:2166-2168 seeds `needed` from fields for childless OUTPUT nodes. For a non-terminal OUTPUT (one that has downstream children), the special case does not apply and the contract claims pass-through; the planner therefore propagates child demand through unchanged, but the runtime select(fields) drops any demanded column not in `fields`, causing a downstream column-not-found. This is a latent gap that only manifests for the unusual topology of an OUTPUT node feeding further nodes; if such topologies are intentionally rejected elsewhere this is moot, but the contract/runtime divergence is concrete and unguarded.
findings.evidence: output_fn l.753-755 selects fields; registration l.743 uses columns=_passthrough_columns; projection.py terminal-only fields seeding at l.2165-2168 (guarded by `if not children`). No fields handling for non-terminal OUTPUT.

findings.title: Stale sys.path comment in _compile_preamble describes idempotent gated inserts the code no longer performs
findings.description: The block comment in _compile_preamble (lines 421-427) states: 'We add both cwd and the pipeline's parent directory ... These inserts are idempotent (gated on `not in sys.path`) so the list doesn't grow on every call.' This is doubly inaccurate. (a) _compile_preamble itself performs NO sys.path mutation — the only sys.path edit in the whole module is in _prioritise_preamble_import_paths (lines 279-280), reached via _compile_preamble_cached. (b) That actual mutation is `sys.path[:] = [existing for existing in sys.path if existing != path]` followed by `sys.path.insert(0, path)` — a remove-then-reinsert, NOT an insert 'gated on `not in sys.path`'. The remove-then-reinsert is what actually prevents growth, while also re-prioritising the entry to position 0 each call (a behaviour the comment does not mention and would be surprising to a maintainer who trusts the 'gated on not in sys.path' description). The stale comment can mislead a maintainer reasoning about import-precedence/ordering during the preamble compile.
findings.evidence: grep for `sys.path` in executor.py returns exactly lines 131 (doc), 279-280 (the only mutation, in _prioritise_preamble_import_paths), and 426 (the stale comment). _compile_preamble's body (380-454) contains no sys.path access; it only computes cwd/pipeline_dir_str/fingerprint and delegates to _compile_preamble_cached, which calls _prioritise_preamble_import_paths under _preamble_lock. The mutation removes all matching entries then inserts at index 0 — neither 'gated on not in sys.path' nor located in _compile_preamble.
findings.est_reduction: ~7 comment lines corrected/removed (no logic change)
findings.behavior_preservation: Comment-only; deleting or correcting it does not alter runtime behaviour.

findings.title: _utility_module_candidates duplicates _cache._utility_candidates_for_dir's utility-path enumeration
findings.description: _utility_module_candidates (executor.py) and _utility_candidates_for_dir (_cache.py) implement the same algorithm: build candidate utility roots from [pipeline_dir?, cwd], then for each base yield `base/'utility.py'` and `base/'utility'`, resolve each, and de-duplicate via a `seen` set preserving order. They produce identical resolved candidate lists. The only textual difference is that _cache's version pre-resolves the pipeline_dir base (`Path(pipeline_dir).resolve()`) while executor's appends `Path(pipeline_dir_str)` unresolved — immaterial because each candidate is resolved in-loop (`candidate.resolve()` resolves the full chain). The two copies serve adjacent concerns (fingerprinting in _cache, on-disk pyc eviction in executor) so they will drift if one is changed (e.g. adding a `utility/` nesting rule) without the other. Consolidating to a single shared helper removes the duplicated dedup/enumeration logic.
findings.evidence: Side-by-side: both functions construct `bases=[pipeline_dir?, cwd.resolve()]`, loop `for candidate in (base/'utility.py', base/'utility')`, `resolved=candidate.resolve()`, skip if in `seen`, else append. Trace shows identical outputs for any input because in-loop `.resolve()` makes the executor's unresolved base immaterial. _utility_module_candidates is consumed only by _evict_utility_import_state (executor.py:256); _utility_candidates_for_dir only by preamble_execution_fingerprint (_cache.py:394).
findings.est_reduction: ~16 lines (one copy of the enumeration body), modulo a cross-module import
findings.behavior_preservation: Both functions already yield byte-identical resolved candidate lists; routing both call sites through one helper preserves the candidate set and ordering, so eviction targets and fingerprint inputs are unchanged.

findings.title: _cached_output_names raises AttributeError on multi-port apiInput parents (dict output has no .columns)
findings.description: _cached_output_names is the schema-warning helper used when an instance node (config['instanceOf']) is present: it sums the columns feeding the instance and the original by calling _cached_output_names(pid) for each parent. For a multi-port apiInput source, _execute_eager_core stores output_columns[nid] = [] and available_columns[nid] = [] (an EMPTY list, not absent) while eager_outputs[nid] is a dict[port_label, DataFrame] (src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1900-1904). In _cached_output_names, `cached = output_cols.get(node_id)` yields [], so `if cached:` is False and it falls through to `df = eager_outputs.get(node_id)` which is the per-port dict, then executes `set(df.columns)` (line 1107). dict has no .columns attribute, so this raises AttributeError. This loop runs inside execute_graph's try/finally that only manages the cache pin — it is NOT covered by the per-node error swallowing of _eager_execute(swallow_errors=True) — so the exception propagates out of execute_graph and fails the entire preview/trace request (HTTP 500) rather than degrading one node. Trigger: a multi-port apiInput wired as a direct parent of any node carrying instanceOf (or of the referenced original). Multi-port apiInput sources and instance nodes are both shipped features and nothing structurally forbids wiring them together.
findings.evidence: executor.py:1103 `cached = output_cols.get(node_id)` -> [] for multi-port; 1104 `if cached:` False (empty list falsy); 1106 `df = eager_outputs.get(node_id)` -> dict (the `materialised` bundle); 1107 `set(df.columns)` -> AttributeError because df is a dict. Population proof: _execute_lazy.py:1900 `eager_outputs[nid] = materialised` (a dict), 1903 `available_columns[nid] = []`, 1904 `output_columns[nid] = []`. Reached via executor.py:1116 / 1120 `_cached_output_names(pid)` for parents of an instanceOf node.

findings.title: _column_infos_for_node reports column_count=0 / columns=[] for a multi-port apiInput's own NodeResult despite a non-empty representative frame
findings.description: For the multi-port apiInput source node, output_columns[nid] is stored as [] (empty list) by the eager core (_execute_lazy.py:1904). In _column_infos_for_node, `full_output = output_cols.get(node_id)` is [] and the guard is `if full_output is not None:` — an empty list is NOT None, so the function takes the empty branch and sets columns = [], never reaching the `elif df is not None:` branch (line 1134) that would correctly read the representative first-port frame's columns. Meanwhile the main results loop (line 1182-1184) reduces the dict to the first port and builds a real preview from it: row_count = len(first_port_df) > 0, preview rows carry the port's columns, and preview_columns is non-empty (line 1208-1221). The resulting NodeResult is internally inconsistent: column_count=0 and columns=[] while preview/preview_columns/row_count reflect a frame that has columns. tests/test_apiinput_multi_port_runtime.py only asserts the CONSUMER nodes' columns, never the multi-port source node's own result, so this silent misreport is untested. This is a classic 'empty-list is not None' bug: the intended fallback to df.columns is dead for the [] case.
findings.evidence: executor.py:1131 `full_output = output_cols.get(node_id)` -> [] ; 1132 `if full_output is not None:` True for [] ; 1133 `columns = [...]` over [] -> columns=[] ; line 1134 `elif df is not None:` (which would read first_port_df.columns) is unreachable when output_cols is []. df passed in is the first-port frame (executor.py:1182-1185). Contrast: a normal node legitimately producing zero columns also hits this branch correctly; only the multi-port case is wrong because its frame has columns but output_columns is [].

findings.title: _eager_execute rebuilds node_map manually instead of using the cached graph.node_map property
findings.description: Line 1327 constructs `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` inside the preamble-error injection block. findings.title: Module constants _VARIABLE_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES and _UNKNOWN_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES are defined but never referenced

findings.title: validate_chunk_capability_declarations silently substitutes the global registry for an explicitly-passed empty mapping (truthiness fallback)
findings.description: Line 348 does `registry = declarations or _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS`. The intent (per the `Mapping | None = None` signature) is 'use the global registry when the caller passes None'. But the `or` test is on truthiness, not `is None`: an explicitly-passed EMPTY mapping `{}` is falsy and is therefore silently replaced by the global `_CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS`. As a result `validate_chunk_capability_declarations({})` validates the global registry (and passes), instead of validating the empty mapping the caller actually handed in (which should fail loudly: it is missing every NodeType). This conflates two distinct inputs ('not provided' vs 'an empty registry') and is precisely the kind of silent fallback the project's CLAUDE.md forbids ('code should be allowed to fail loudly... a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice'). A validator that cannot detect a completely-empty registry is a contract hole: a future refactor that builds the registry dynamically and accidentally yields `{}` would pass this guard rather than being caught.
findings.evidence: Line 348: `registry = declarations or _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS`. For `declarations={}`: `{} or _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS` evaluates to `_CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS` because `{}` is falsy, so `expected - observed` (line 351-352) is computed against the full global registry and `missing`/`extra` are both empty -> no RuntimeError raised. The drift test at tests/test_chunk_plan.py:99-104 only ever passes a 17-entry dict (POLARS popped from the 18-entry registry), which is still truthy, so it never exercises the empty-mapping path; the empty case is unguarded. The correct, fail-loud form is `registry = _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS if declarations is None else declarations`, which would raise the existing 'must mention every node type exactly once' RuntimeError for `{}` (Missing=all 18 node types).

findings.title: Manual unlink of dest/.parquet.tmp in _write_chunk_checkpoint failure path is unreachable-as-effective; atomic_write already guarantees removal
findings.description: On a checkpoint write failure, _write_chunk_checkpoint's except block calls `path.unlink(missing_ok=True)` and `path.with_suffix('.parquet.tmp').unlink(missing_ok=True)` before rmdir. Neither call can ever find a file to remove. `atomic_write` (src/haute/_polars_utils.py:288-293) wraps the write in `try: yield tmp; tmp.replace(dest) except BaseException: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise`, so on ANY exception inside the `with` body (the only failure point is `frame.write_parquet(tmp, ...)`) the temp file is already unlinked by atomic_write before control returns to _write_chunk_checkpoint. The final `dest` is created only by the atomic `tmp.replace(dest)`, which runs solely on the success path and is itself atomic (os.replace cannot partially create dest), so `path` (dest) never exists on the failure path either. Thus both unlink calls are guaranteed no-ops. The only load-bearing cleanup in this block is the `checkpoint_dir.rmdir()` (which removes the now-empty owned dir on a first-chunk failure). The redundant unlinks are confirmed non-load-bearing by the passing regression test test_chunk_runner_cleans_partial_checkpoint_write_failure (tests/test_chunk_runner.py:890-914), which writes a partial tmp file then raises and still passes purely via atomic_write's own cleanup.
findings.evidence: _polars_utils.py atomic_write: `try: yield tmp; tmp.replace(dest) except BaseException: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise` -> tmp always removed on failure, dest never created on failure. chunking.py:1552-1556: `with atomic_write(path) as tmp: frame.write_parquet(...) except BaseException: path.unlink(missing_ok=True); path.with_suffix('.parquet.tmp').unlink(missing_ok=True); ...` -> at this point tmp is already gone and dest absent, so both unlinks match nothing in every reachable path (write_parquet failure, or the atomic replace failure).
findings.est_reduction: -2 LOC (drop the two redundant unlink statements at 1555-1556; keep the rmdir cleanup). Net: removes dead defensive cleanup, leaving atomic_write as the single source of temp/dest cleanup.
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior is identical: the two unlinks are provable no-ops in all reachable failure paths because atomic_write unconditionally unlinks the temp file and never creates dest on failure. The kept rmdir and the outer _cleanup_written_checkpoints path are unaffected. test_chunk_runner_cleans_partial_checkpoint_write_failure already proves cleanup succeeds without relying on these unlinks.

findings.description: iter_chunked_frames performs a function-local `from haute._polars_utils import (bounded_collect_batches, streaming_collect, temporary_streaming_chunk_size)`. However `streaming_collect` is already imported at module scope on line 27 (`from haute._polars_utils import DEFAULT_STREAMING_CHUNK_SIZE, streaming_collect`) and is used elsewhere in the module at lines 670 and 1029 via that module-level binding. Only `bounded_collect_batches` and `temporary_streaming_chunk_size` genuinely need the local import (they are not imported at module level). This is incidental redundancy, not a correctness issue.

Line 864 re-imports the same `streaming_collect` inside iter_chunked_frames. grep of `streaming_collect` in chunking.py shows usages at 670 and 1029 (both resolvable from the module-level import) plus the redundant local import at 864.

findings.title: Type-mismatch list silently truncated to 10 with no "... and N more" indicator (inconsistent with the missing-features block)
findings.description: _format_feature_mismatch renders the missing-feature block with an explicit overflow line (`if n_missing > 20: lines.append(f'  ... and {n_missing - 20} more')`, lines 179-180) but the type-mismatch block iterates `type_mismatches[:10]` (line 185) with NO equivalent overflow notice. When a wide model is scored with more than 10 declared-categorical columns each supplied as a numeric dtype, the operator is told to 'fix the upstream schema or re-train' but the diagnostic shows only the first 10 offending columns and gives no signal that further columns are also mis-typed. The truncation is real: the type-mismatch raise (lines 256-267) fires precisely when `usable` is non-empty and nothing is missing, i.e. all expected features are present but >=1 categorical was passed numeric — a wide model can easily exceed 10 such columns. The result is a fail-loud error whose remediation guidance is silently incomplete, so the operator may fix the 10 shown columns, re-run, and hit the same error again on the next 10.
findings.evidence: Lines 175-187: missing block has `for name in missing[:20]: ...` followed by `if n_missing > 20: lines.append(f'  ... and {n_missing - 20} more')`. Type block (183-187): `lines.append('Type mismatch(es):'); for col, expected_type, actual_type in type_mismatches[:10]: lines.append(...)` then `lines.append('')` — no `if len(type_mismatches) > 10` overflow line. `n_missing` is computed (line 167) but there is no `n_type_mismatches`. The header count uses `n_expected`/`n_available` only, so the total type-mismatch count is never surfaced anywhere in the message.
