findings.title: _normalise_frontier_range_pair raises raw Python float() messages (TypeError / unprefixed ValueError) on the config-side path, breaking its documented "error messages match" contract
findings.description: The function's docstring states it is the 'single source of truth for both the request-body schema layer and the config-side path' so error wording is shared. That promise holds for the tested cases (missing keys, non-finite, min>max) because they are explicit string-keyed raises. It does NOT hold when a min/max value is a non-numeric scalar or a nested value, because float(raw_min)/float(raw_max) on line 63-64 raise Python's own exceptions instead of a field-prefixed ValueError. Two concrete cases on the config path (which passes RAW, un-coerced JSON values from config['frontier_ranges'] into _normalise_frontier_range in _optimiser_service._auto_frontier_ranges_from_config): (a) a string min/max, e.g. frontier_ranges={'volume': ['abc','def']}, yields ValueError 'could not convert string to float: \'abc\'' rather than 'frontier_ranges.volume must contain ...'; (b) a nested min/max, e.g. {'volume': {'min': [1,2], 'max': 3}}, raises TypeError 'float() argument must be a string or a real number, not \'list\''. The request-body path (OptimiserFrontierRequest.threshold_ranges) is NOT affected because pydantic's list[float] coercion runs before the mode='after' validator and rejects/converts those inputs first (verified: validator only ever sees pre-coerced floats). So this is config-path-only. The TypeError is ultimately caught by the broad `except Exception` at _optimiser_service.py:2232 and surfaced as a non-fatal 'Frontier unavailable: <raw msg>' frontier_error, so it does not crash the worker, but the user sees an internal float() message instead of the intended, consistent field-scoped diagnostic the function was written to provide.
findings.evidence: Line 63-64: `min_value = float(raw_min); max_value = float(raw_max)` with no try/except; the structured ValueErrors only guard None (line 60-61), shape (line 57-58), finiteness (line 65-66) and ordering (line 67-68). Confirmed at runtime: `_normalise_frontier_range_pair(['abc','def'], field='threshold_ranges.volume')` -> ValueError "could not convert string to float: 'abc'"; `_normalise_frontier_range_pair({'min':[1,2],'max':3}, field='frontier_ranges.volume')` -> TypeError (not a ValueError, so it escapes the function's own error model). Config-side caller: _optimiser_service.py:1386 ranges[...] = _normalise_frontier_range(configured_ranges[cname], ...) on raw dict values; wrapped by `except Exception` at line 2232.

findings.title: _normalise_frontier_range_pair silently accepts booleans as range bounds (e.g. [False, True] -> (0.0, 1.0)) on the config path, inconsistent with the sibling _reject_bool_chunk_size policy
findings.description: Because bool is a subclass of int, float(False)==0.0 and float(True)==1.0, and booleans pass the finiteness and ordering checks. So a frontier-range value of [False, True] (or {'min': False, 'max': True}) is silently normalised to the numeric range (0.0, 1.0) instead of being rejected as a malformed payload. This is the opposite policy from the file's own sibling validator _reject_bool_chunk_size (lines 21-24), which was deliberately added to reject bool for streaming_chunk_size on the grounds that a bool is almost certainly a client bug rather than a real number. As with finding 1, the request-body path (OptimiserFrontierRequest.threshold_ranges, list[float]) is unaffected because pydantic coerces [False,True] to [0.0,1.0] before the after-validator runs; the silent acceptance is reachable on the config-side path (_auto_frontier_ranges_from_config) where raw JSON booleans flow straight in. Severity is low because boolean range bounds in an optimiser config are a degenerate, low-probability input, but it is a genuine validation gap and an inconsistency with the module's stated bool-rejection stance for numeric fields.
findings.evidence: Runtime: `_normalise_frontier_range_pair([False, True], field='x')` returns (0.0, 1.0); `_normalise_frontier_range_pair({'min': False, 'max': True}, field='x')` returns (0.0, 1.0). No isinstance(..., bool) guard exists in the function, whereas the adjacent _reject_bool_chunk_size (line 22) does `if isinstance(value, bool): raise ValueError(...)`. isinstance(True, int) is True, so the int-based float() coercion accepts bools.

coverage.notes: Sole in-scope function is OptimiserFrontierRequest._validate_threshold_ranges (src/haute/schemas.py:1085-1099), a mode='after' field_validator. It iterates value.items() and delegates each range to the shared canonical helper _normalise_frontier_range_pair (schemas.py:45-69), which validates element count (==2), None-ness, finiteness (math.isfinite), and ordering (min<=max). The field is typed dict[str,list[float]] so Pydantic coerces each value to list[float] before the validator runs; the helper's dict-form branch is unreachable from this call site but is shared with the config-side path (_optimiser_service.py _auto_frontier_ranges_from_config), so it is not dead overall. Edge cases verified clean: empty dict -> returns {} (default), wrong-length lists -> rejected, NaN/Inf -> coerced via allow_inf_nan then rejected by isfinite, inverted range -> rejected. All four cases are covered by tests/test_optimiser_contracts.py:657-681. Discarding the normalised tuple and returning the raw list[float] is intentional and documented (lines 1092-1094); downstream optimiser.py:355-359 correctly re-tuples to (float(v[0]), float(v[1])), so no contract violation. The function is already minimal (no over-complexity, duplication, or dead code) and the delegation to a single source-of-truth helper is sound engineering. The only adjacent observation -- the request-body field type forbids the dict {min,max} form that the config path accepts -- is explicitly documented as intentional ('list[float] for JSON-payload simplicity') and is behavior-correct, so not reported as a defect. No new findings beyond the known catalog entry.

findings.title: _format_contract_source silently overwrites inputs_by_parent when a parent-id key and that parent's emitted func-name appear as two separate declared keys
findings.description: When serialising a declared contract's inputs_by_parent, each declared key is reclassified: an id present in parent_name_by_id is remapped to its emitted func-name (line 142-143), while a key already equal to one of the emitted func-names is kept verbatim (line 144-145). Both branches then write `inputs_by_parent[emitted_parent] = ...` (line 149). If the same physical parent is represented by BOTH its node-id key (e.g. 'left-uuid') AND its already-resolved func-name key (e.g. 'Left_Input') in the declared contract, both reduce to emitted_parent='Left_Input' and the loop assignment last-writer-wins, silently dropping one entry's column set. The winner is decided purely by `sorted(contract.inputs_by_parent.items())` key order, so which columns survive is arbitrary and the loss is silent (no warning, no error) — exactly the silent-wrongness class the project guidelines forbid.
findings.evidence: Loop at 139-149: parent_id in parent_name_by_id -> emitted_parent = name (143); elif parent_id in parent_names (the set of func-names, line 136) -> emitted_parent = parent_id (kept, 145); line 149 `inputs_by_parent[emitted_parent] = None if columns is None else sorted(columns)`. With declared inputs_by_parent = {'left-uuid': [A], 'Left_Input': [B]} and parent_name_by_id = {'left-uuid':'Left_Input'} (per test_graph_to_code_remaps_inputs_by_parent_ids_to_function_names, tests/test_codegen_fail_loudly.py:104-155, distinct labels guarantee distinct func-names via _error_on_name_collisions): 'Left_Input' is in parent_names so it is kept; 'left-uuid' remaps to 'Left_Input'; both assign inputs_by_parent['Left_Input'], so sorting puts 'Left_Input' before 'left-uuid' and the id-derived [A] overwrites the name-keyed [B] (or vice versa depending on inputs). No collision detection exists; the result is emitted as the file's contract and consumed by projection.declared_inputs_by_parent (projection.py:1784-1821), so the wrong/narrowed parent-column ownership is persisted. A mixed id+name keyed inputs_by_parent is reachable by re-saving a file whose inputs_by_parent was already name-keyed by a prior save while config still carries an id-keyed entry, or by a hand-authored/partially-migrated contract.

findings.title: Dead `if declared is not None:` branch in _format_contract_kwarg — Contract.from_user_declared can never return None once declared_raw is not None
findings.description: Line 96 already guards `if declared_raw is not None:` before calling `declared = Contract.from_user_declared(declared_raw)` (line 97). Contract.from_user_declared returns None ONLY for a None input (haute/_contracts.py:65); every other input either returns a Contract or raises ValueError (it never returns None for a non-None value). Therefore line 98 `if declared is not None:` is always True, and the implicit else (fall through to the get_column_contract path) is unreachable. The defensive guard suggests a fall-through that cannot occur, obscuring the actual control flow (a malformed declared contract raises, it does not silently fall through to contract recomputation).
findings.evidence: _contracts.py Contract.from_user_declared: `if value is None: return None` (65) is the sole None return; '' -> raises (78), {} -> raises (93-96), [] -> raises (105), any unknown type -> raises (105). Given codegen.py:96 already excludes None, `declared` at line 98 is never None. The branch's else (continuing to line 100 try/get_column_contract) can never be taken when declared_raw is truthy.
findings.est_reduction: ~1 line (collapse the redundant guard) + removes a misleading apparent fall-through path
findings.behavior_preservation: Replacing `if declared is not None: return _format_contract_source(...)` with an unconditional `return _format_contract_source(...)` is behaviour-identical because declared is provably non-None here; no input reaches the recompute path via this branch today.

findings.title: graph_to_code() silently returns the FIRST submodel file (not the main pipeline) when given a graph with submodels
findings.description: graph_to_code delegates to graph_to_code_multi and does `return next(iter(files.values()))`, documented as 'returns the single generated file's code'. That assumption only holds for submodel-free graphs. When the graph has submodels, graph_to_code_multi returns a multi-entry dict whose submodel files are inserted FIRST (line 1097, inside the per-submodel loop) and the main pipeline file LAST (line 1262). Since Python dicts preserve insertion order, next(iter(files.values())) returns the first submodel module's source, NOT the main pipeline. The public API thus returns the wrong artifact with no error. The unstated single-file precondition is neither asserted nor handled: it should either fail loudly when len(files) != 1 or explicitly select the main file. This is the kind of silent-wrong-result that should fail loudly per the project's 'no incorrect fallbacks' rule.
findings.evidence: graph_to_code: files = graph_to_code_multi(...); return next(iter(files.values())). In graph_to_code_multi the submodel branch builds files[sm_file] = ... at line 1097 (loop over submodels, runs first), then files[main_key] = ... at line 1262 (runs last). With submodels present, iter(files.values()) yields the submodel code first. The sole production caller (src/haute/routes/_save_pipeline.py:517-535) guards with `if graph.submodels: graph_to_code_multi(...) else: graph_to_code(...)`, so production is safe; but graph_to_code is exported in __all__ (codegen.py:49-52) and is a documented public entry point, so a direct caller passing a submodel graph silently gets the wrong file. Tests only call graph_to_code on flat graphs (e.g. tests/test_submodel.py:231 uses flat_graph), so this path is currently unexercised.

findings.title: Submodel cross-boundary handle validation is hand-rolled twice, duplicating _resolve_submodel_endpoint
findings.description: graph_to_code_multi validates submodel boundary handles in three places that share identical logic: (a) the inline input loop at 1013-1043 (checks handle.startswith('in__'), slices child_id, checks membership in sm_child_ids, raises the same two ParseError messages), (b) the inline output-validation loop at 1044-1068 (same for 'out__'), and (c) the _resolve_submodel_endpoint closure at 1117-1150 which performs exactly this validation for both prefixes and raises the same two ParseError messages. The closure was clearly introduced to centralize this, but the two earlier loops were never folded into it. Moreover the 1044-1068 loop is pure validation with no output: every edge whose source == submodel placeholder is later re-validated by _resolve_submodel_endpoint(prefix='out__') in the root_node_sources loop (1163) and root_connect_pairs loop (1202), so loop (b) is fully redundant. The input loop (a) only additionally accumulates src_name into sm_node_sources; its validation half duplicates the helper.
findings.evidence: Lines 1017-1037 (in__ validation + child_id membership + ParseError 'missing or malformed targetHandle' / 'references a child node that does not exist') are byte-for-byte the same checks and messages as _resolve_submodel_endpoint lines 1128-1149. Lines 1048-1068 (out__ variant) duplicate the same helper for prefix='out__'. For any edge with source=='submodel__sm', _resolve_submodel_endpoint(edge, src, sh, prefix='out__', endpoint='source') at line 1163/1202 re-runs identical startswith/child_id/membership validation, so the 1044-1068 loop adds no checks not already enforced downstream. The only behavioural difference is the submodel= kwarg value (sm_name vs node_id.removeprefix('submodel__')), which are equal.
findings.behavior_preservation: Refactoring loop (a) to call _resolve_submodel_endpoint for the in__ resolution (keeping only the src_name accumulation) and deleting the redundant loop (b) preserves behavior: the same handles are validated with the same ParseError types/messages, just once. The redundant out__ loop's only effect is raising on malformed out__ handles, which _resolve_submodel_endpoint already does at the same point in the same call (before any file is emitted), so no error is lost.
findings.est_reduction: ~35-45 lines

findings.title: Two consecutive edge loops recompute identical _resolve_submodel_endpoint results for every edge
findings.description: The root_node_sources loop (1156-1183) and the root_connect_pairs loop (1195-1235) each iterate `for edge in edges` and independently compute actual_src = _resolve_submodel_endpoint(edge, src, sh, prefix='out__', ...) and actual_tgt = _resolve_submodel_endpoint(edge, tgt, th, prefix='in__', ...) with identical arguments, then derive src_func/tgt_func the same way (root_id_to_func.get(actual_*, _sanitize_func_name(actual_*))). The only difference is loop 1 filters to actual_tgt in root_node_ids and records sources, while loop 2 records connect pairs for all edges. The boundary resolution (which also re-raises on malformed handles) is therefore performed twice per edge. Merging into a single pass over edges that computes actual_src/actual_tgt/src_func/tgt_func once and feeds both root_node_sources/root_node_source_ids and root_connect_pairs would remove the duplicated resolution and the second identical raise-path.
findings.evidence: Loop 1 lines 1163-1176 and Loop 2 lines 1202-1215 contain the same four _resolve_submodel_endpoint(...) calls with the same parameters; src_func/tgt_func derivation at 1181 and 1217-1218 is identical. Both loops read the same `edges` list with no mutation in between, so per-edge resolution is deterministic and recomputed.
findings.behavior_preservation: Combining the two loops into one pass yields identical root_node_sources, root_node_source_ids and root_connect_pairs (same append order, same filter on root_node_ids for sources, no filter for connect pairs). _resolve_submodel_endpoint is pure and raises deterministically, so doing the resolution once per edge raises on exactly the same malformed edges at the same stage.
findings.est_reduction: ~20-25 lines

coverage.notes: Exhaustively reviewed all 28 in-scope functions (lines 1-626) plus context functions (_buffer_to_frame, build_per_port_cache, _swap_dir_into_place, load_per_port_cache, load_v2_api_source, is_per_port_cache_valid, infer_v2_schema_from_data) and the _api_input_schema.py dependencies (validate_v2_schema, parse_table_path, parse_column_path, sanitise_label_for_filesystem). No NEW reportable defects beyond the known catalog. Candidate observations evaluated and DELIBERATELY NOT reported: (1) _v2_fingerprint sorts tables by `path` only (lambda t: t.get('path') or ''), not a total order when two tables legitimately share a path (validate_v2_schema enforces label uniqueness but NOT path uniqueness) — Python's stable sort then preserves differing editor input-order, so reordering two same-path tables changes the fingerprint; this only causes a SPURIOUS cache rebuild (errs toward rebuilding = safe, never stale-serving) and is in the same family as the known _v2_fingerprint findings and the documented `levels`-over-inclusion concern (region-maps.json:831), so not worth a separate finding. (2) _BUILD_LOCKS dict (line 283) is never pruned — a lock registry that grows monotonically per distinct resolved cache dir; documented as process-local by design, cardinality naturally bounded by distinct (data-hash, schema) cache dirs in this app, a standard accepted idiom = not a real leak. Verified the hand-rolled streaming JSON parser (_iter_sampled_json_array_records / _read_root_array_value / _validate_eof) is correct for: empty arrays, trailing commas after both scalars and objects, EOF detection, trailing-data rejection, multibyte UTF-8 inside strings (byte-level copy is UTF-8 safe), escaped quotes/backslashes inside strings, scalars-with-whitespace-before-delimiter (rstrip), sample-boundary stop with interleaved non-object elements, and BOM (loud-fails consistently in both sampled and full paths). Verified _read_non_ws handles EOF before the `b not in b' \t\r\n'` membership test (avoiding the empty-bytes-is-substring trap via the `not b` short-circuit). Verified _coerce_scalar int/float/str/bool/None paths and that an int-typed scalar column has no widening branch (ints pass through, any float would loud-fail in _buffer_to_frame). Verified _walk null-element vs null-key distinction, scalar-vs-object table shape skip-counting, and deterministic row ordering. All headline correctness bugs (mid-walk list collapse, nested-list row inflation, size+mtime fast-path staleness, non-dict fingerprint collision, scalar-array inference over-widening, unvalidated-config status path) are already in the known catalog.

findings.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1199-1221 (infer_v2_schema_from_data column assembly; the object-table branch `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` at :1213) interacting with the reserved sentinel `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF` (:72) consumed in shred_to_buffers._walk at :629-632
findings.title: A literal JSON key named "$value" collides with the reserved scalar-array sentinel, so inference emits a $value-leaf column on an OBJECT table and shred_to_buffers silently drops EVERY record of that table
findings.description: The module reserves the leaf token `$value` (`_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`) to mean "the scalar element itself" for scalar-array child tables, and the header comment (lines 70-71) asserts "a JSON key can't be `$value` in this path grammar, so there's no collision with a real field." That assertion is false. `infer_v2_schema_from_data` builds an object column's path as `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with NO escaping/guarding of `col_name`, so a record carrying a real key `"$value"` yields an object-table column with path `$[*].$value`. At shred time `parse_column_path` returns the leaf `$value`, which EQUALS `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`. In `shred_to_buffers._walk`, `is_scalar_table = any(leaf == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF ...)` (line 629) then becomes TRUE for what is actually an OBJECT table, so the shape guard `if is_scalar_table != (not is_dict)` (line 630) treats every dict record as a shape mismatch and `continue`s past it (counting it as a skipped row). The whole table emits ZERO rows. Because validate_v2_schema accepts `$value` as a legal leaf and `_v2_fingerprint` sees a distinct path, the cache is judged valid/fresh; the only signal is the skipped-rows counter (which the user must notice). This is distinct from the catalogued 'scalar-value-column-fixed-name-ambiguity' finding (that is about output-port identity / a real field named `value` being indistinguishable downstream); here the *sentinel* `$value` causes total, silent row loss on the build path.
findings.evidence: Reproduced end-to-end: records=[{"$value":10,"other":1},{"$value":20,"other":2}] -> infer_v2_schema_from_data emits root column path '$[*].$value'; parse_column_path('$[*].$value','$[*]') == '$value' == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF (True). build_per_port_cache + load_per_port_cache -> root frame height=0 (columns ['$value','other']) from 2 source records; shred_to_buffers skip stats = {'records':0,'rows_by_table':{'$[*]':2}}. Trace: _walk line 629 is_scalar_table=True for a dict record (is_dict=True), line 630 True != (not True=False) -> True -> _count_row_skip + continue, so no row is ever appended.

findings.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1203/1213 (infer_v2_schema_from_data builds column path `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with an unescaped key) consumed by _resolve_leaf dotted-walk at :526-536
findings.title: infer_v2_schema_from_data manufactures a dotted column path for a JSON key that literally contains a dot, so the shred silently resolves the value to None (value lost, not even counted as a skip)
findings.description: Inference emits an object column whose path is `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with no escaping of `col_name`. For a record with a key that itself contains a dot (e.g. `"a.b": 42`), this yields column path `$[*].a.b`, and `parse_column_path` returns the leaf `a.b`. The dotted leaf is then interpreted by `_resolve_leaf` (lines 526-536) as a NESTED path: it walks `value.get("a")` then `.get("b")`, which is absent (the real key is the single string `"a.b"`), so the column resolves to None. The original value is silently lost and the row is still emitted with None (so it is not surfaced by skip accounting either). The schema also round-trips through validate_v2_schema cleanly, hiding the problem. This shares the `_resolve_leaf` dotted-ambiguity root with catalogued finding #12/BUG-N3 (a list at an intermediate dotted segment), but the NEW angle is that inference itself fabricates these ambiguous flat-key-as-dotted-path columns with no guard, making it reachable from the ordinary Infer Tables -> Cache as Parquet flow rather than only from hand-authored configs.

findings.title: Generated GitLab CI uv cache never caches anything (wrong cache path)
findings.description: gitlab_ci_yml() emits a default cache block with `paths: - .cache/uv`, but uv does NOT write its cache to a project-relative `.cache/uv` directory. By default uv caches to a home/XDG location (`~/.cache/uv` on Linux, confirmed `uv cache dir` -> AppData/.cache outside the repo). GitLab CI `cache.paths` are resolved relative to `$CI_PROJECT_DIR`, and paths outside the build directory cannot be cached, so the configured cache silently captures an empty/nonexistent directory and every pipeline re-downloads dependencies. The GitHub and Azure templates do not have this problem (GitHub uses `astral-sh/setup-uv@v4` with `enable-cache: true`, which targets uv's real cache dir; Azure configures no uv cache). The fix is to point uv at the cached dir, e.g. add `UV_CACHE_DIR: .cache/uv` to the top-level `variables`/`default.variables` so uv actually writes there.
findings.evidence: default.cache.paths = ['.cache/uv'] (lines 606-609) and before_script runs `pip install "uv>=0.5,<1" && uv sync --frozen` (line 611) with no UV_CACHE_DIR set. `uv cache dir` resolves to C:\Users\...\AppData\Local\uv\cache (home, not project); on Linux runners it is ~/.cache/uv, outside $CI_PROJECT_DIR, so GitLab cannot persist it. test_caching only asserts the literal '.cache/uv' substring is present, never that caching is effective.

findings.title: _ModelCacheWithCascade.put skips the validation-cache cascade when a key is overwritten in place
findings.description: `_ModelCacheWithCascade.put` detects evicted models by diffing the pre-put key snapshot (`before`) against the post-put key set (`after_keys`) and treating `k not in after_keys` as 'was evicted'. This correctly catches LRU capacity evictions (the evicted key disappears from `_data`), but it MISSES the case where `put` is called with a key that already exists and a *different* `ScoringModel` value. The base `LRUCache.put` overwrites in place (`self._data[key] = value`, lines _lru_cache.py:160-164), so the key remains in `after_keys`; the diff yields no evicted models, and `_ms._invalidate_feature_validation_cache_for(old_model)` is never invoked for the replaced object. Consequently the feature-validation cache in `_model_scorer` retains entries keyed on `id(old_model)` (key shape `(id(scoring_model), contract, schema)`, _model_scorer.py:72/317-321). Those entries are now unreachable garbage that linger until LRU pressure or a full `clear()` removes them — the exact leak the targeted cascade was built to prevent (docstring _model_scorer.py:138-148: 'purge them so the table does not fill with dead id() values'). The method's own docstring (lines 144-147) promises 'every eviction triggers the targeted ... hook', so the in-place-replacement value drop is a contract violation.
findings.evidence: Override put (lines 157-171): `before = dict(self._data); super().put(key, value); after_keys = set(self._data); evicted_models = [v for k, v in before.items() if k not in after_keys]`. For an overwrite of an existing key K, K is in both `before` and `after_keys`, so `evicted_models` is empty even though `before[K]` (the old ScoringModel) was just dropped by base put's `self._data[key] = value`. The validation entries keyed on `id(before[K])` are never invalidated. Tests in tests/test_feature_validation_cache.py (TestValidationCacheCascadeEviction) exercise LRU eviction, targeted invalidation, and full clear, but never the same-key overwrite path, so the gap is untested.
findings.behavior_preservation: Reachability through load_mlflow_model is low because the get-then-put sequence is serialized under _artifact_io_lock(run_id, artifact_path) and same-key callers see a get-hit before reaching put; production therefore rarely (if ever) overwrites a live key with a new object. The defect is a latent contract gap in the general-purpose put method (leak, not wrong result, since a stale id-keyed entry only produces a false get-hit if the reused id ALSO collides on contract+schema). A correct fix would diff on value identity for retained keys (e.g. invalidate when before[k] is not self._data[k]) and add a same-key-overwrite cascade test.

findings.title: Fast-path cache key drops `version` while the canonical key keeps it, so run-sourced catboost/rustystats models load from disk twice and leave a permanently-orphaned duplicate cache entry (and skewed hit/miss counters); pyfunc loses the fast path entirely
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a
findings.description: load_mlflow_model has two cache-key construction sites that disagree for `source_type="run"` whenever a non-empty `version` is supplied. The fast-path (lines 893-900) hardcodes `version=""`, so `_model_cache_key` (lines 311-313: truthy version -> 5-tuple, else 4-tuple) returns the 4-tuple `("run", run_id, artifact_path, task)`. The slow-path (lines 968-974) passes `version=resolved_version`, and for a run source `resolve_mlflow_source` returns `resolved_version = version` unchanged (_mlflow_utils.py:101,109-111). Production callers ALWAYS pass `version=config.get("version", "latest")` even for run sources (src/haute/_builders.py:1196; src/haute/_model_explainability.py:569; threaded through ModelScorer._load_scoring_model_uncached at _model_scorer.py:1063-1070). With `version="latest"` (truthy) the slow-path stores the model under the 5-tuple `("run", run_id, "latest", artifact_path, task)` while the fast-path only ever looks up / stores the 4-tuple. The two keys can never coincide. CONSEQUENCES for catboost/rustystats (the only in-repo producers): call 1 (cold) misses the 4-tuple, finds no disk file, falls to the slow path, downloads + loads + put(5-tuple); call 2 misses the 4-tuple again (model is under the 5-tuple), now finds the disk file present and re-loads it from disk via the disk-cache fast path, put(4-tuple) — so the model is deserialized from disk TWICE before steady state, TWO cache MISSES are recorded for one logical model (skewing get_model_cache_stats hit-rate), and the 5-tuple entry becomes dead weight that the steady-state fast path never hits again, permanently consuming one of only _MODEL_CACHE_MAX_SIZE=16 slots until LRU-evicted (effectively halving cache capacity for run-sourced models). For pyfunc run-sourced models the disk-cache fast-path block is skipped entirely (it is gated on `flavor in ("catboost","rustystats")` at line 910), so the 4-tuple lookup at line 901 ALWAYS misses and EVERY call falls through to resolve_mlflow_source() — defeating the very tracking-server round-trip the fast path exists to avoid (per the comment at lines 888-892). No price-correctness impact (same model bytes, same run_id+artifact_path), but it is a real cache-coherence defect: redundant disk loads, a permanently duplicated/orphaned cache entry, defeated fast-path, and inaccurate observability counters.

Slow-path: line 968-974 `cache_key = _model_cache_key(... version=resolved_version ...)`; resolve_mlflow_source returns resolved_version=version for run source (_mlflow_utils.py:100-101 `resolved_version = version`, and the `elif source_type == "run"` branch at 109-111 never reassigns it). Caller default: _builders.py:1196 `version=config.get("version", "latest")` (passed to ModelScorer.version -> _load_scoring_model_uncached -> load_mlflow_model). For a run source with version="latest": fast_key=4-tuple, cache_key=5-tuple -> disjoint. Disk-cache fast-path put(fast_key) at line 936 vs slow-path put(cache_key) at line 1028 store under different keys; the gate at line 910 (`if flavor in ("catboost", "rustystats")`) is why pyfunc never reaches the disk-cache fast path and thus always falls through to the network resolve. Not in the two known findings (which concern training-vs-scored prediction semantics and the pyfunc loader_module missing _load_pyfunc symbol) and not in the catalog (which covers output-schema/deploy version staleness, not this intra-function fast/slow key split).

findings.title: clear_model_cache(run_id=...) rmtree's a run's disk-cache directory without holding `_disk_cache_run_in_use` or the per-artifact I/O lock, violating the module's own eviction-safety invariant and racing a concurrent load of the same run
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a
findings.description: Every other disk-cache mutation in this module is serialized against in-flight loads: _evict_disk_cache snapshots `_active_disk_cache_runs()` and re-checks `_disk_cache_active_runs` under its guard before each rmtree (lines 589-602), and download/move/corrupt-retry-delete all run under `_artifact_io_lock(run_id, artifact_path)` wrapped in `_disk_cache_run_in_use(run_id)` (e.g. lines 911-918, 1016). clear_model_cache(run_id=...) does NOT participate in either mechanism: at lines 734-737 it computes `target = cache_root / run_id` and calls `shutil.rmtree(target, ignore_errors=True)` with no `_disk_cache_run_in_use` increment and no `_artifact_io_lock`. A concurrent load_mlflow_model for the same run can therefore observe `local_path.is_file()` True (line 643 or 917), then have the directory rmtree'd out from under it before load_local_model() opens the file, surfacing a spurious FileNotFoundError; or the loader's `cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` + `shutil.move` (lines 685-686) can interleave with the rmtree and leave a half-deleted run directory. Because rmtree uses ignore_errors=True the partial deletion is silent. Severity is low: clear_model_cache is operator-invoked, the load failure is recovered by _load_with_bounded_retry's re-download, and prices are never wrong — but it is a genuine inconsistency with the eviction-safety invariant the rest of the module is built around (the disk-eviction path went to lengths to be race-safe; the targeted clear bypasses all of it).
findings.evidence: clear_model_cache run_id branch (lines 733-737): `target = cache_root / run_id; if target.exists(): removed = ...; shutil.rmtree(target, ignore_errors=True)` — no `with _disk_cache_run_in_use(run_id)` and no `with _artifact_io_lock(run_id, ...)` anywhere in the function (the only guarded access in the function is `_validate_disk_cache_run_id` at line 728 and the in-memory `_model_cache.evict_matching` at line 757). Contrast _evict_disk_cache (lines 589-602) which both excludes `_active_disk_cache_runs()` from candidates AND re-checks `if d.name in _disk_cache_active_runs: continue` under `_disk_cache_active_runs_guard` before rmtree, and the loader paths that hold `_artifact_io_lock` while touching the same files. findings.title: _sanitize_description's leading-\n heuristic corrupts single-line descriptions that have leading whitespace, and still drops trailing newlines/blank-lines (cleandoc strips them); these input classes are outside the existing round-trip test matrix
findings.description: The sanitiser prepends a newline when `'\n' in desc or desc != desc.strip()` to neutralise inspect.cleandoc's first-line handling. But cleandoc ALSO strips the minimum common indentation of every line after the first. For a single-line description with leading whitespace (e.g. ' hello'), the prepend makes that text the 'second line', so cleandoc strips its leading indent and the leading whitespace is silently lost on round-trip. findings.title: _gen_model_score drops runtime-affecting categorical_levels and feature_contract_path from the emitted decorator, silently losing categorical-domain / feature-contract validation on a parse->re-save round-trip
findings.description: _gen_model_score builds decorator_kwargs from a HAND-PICKED allowlist (sourceType/run_id/artifact_path/registered_model/version/task/output_column, plus optional run_name/experiment_name/experiment_id) and never emits two persisted ModelScoreConfig keys that DO affect scoring: categorical_levels (_types.py:180) and feature_contract_path (_types.py:179). Both are consumed at runtime by score_from_config (_model_scorer.py:1252-1253: feature_contract_path=cfg.get('feature_contract_path') or None; categorical_levels=cfg.get('categorical_levels') or None), which drives categorical value-domain enforcement and feature-contract checks in ModelScorer. At the FIRST save the sidecar JSON is written from the node config via _prepare_config_for_sidecar (both keys are in VALID_KEYS[MODEL_SCORE] because categorical_levels is a _UNIVERSAL_KEY and feature_contract_path is a ModelScoreConfig field), so the runtime body recovers them from the sidecar and behaves correctly. The loss is silent and occurs on any parse->re-save cycle: when the generated .py is re-parsed by parse_pipeline_source, _config_builder._build_config (_config_builder.py:111-116) rebuilds the model_score config from decorator kwargs ONLY (it does not read the existing sidecar). Because the decorator omitted both keys, the rebuilt node config lacks them; on the next save, _prepare_config_for_sidecar derives the sidecar from that now-incomplete config and the sidecar loses categorical_levels/feature_contract_path -> score_from_config stops applying categorical-domain / feature-contract validation. categorical_levels is the stronger half: the parser explicitly supports restoring it (MODEL_SCORE_CONFIG_KEYS at _types.py:487-499 includes categorical_levels), and _gen_api_input demonstrably PRESERVES categorical_levels (asserted by tests/test_codegen_builders.py:115-128 'test_api_input_preserves_categorical_levels_in_shared_reader'), so the omission in _gen_model_score is an inconsistency, not an intentional design choice. (feature_contract_path is additionally absent from MODEL_SCORE_CONFIG_KEYS, so even were it emitted the parser would not restore it -- but the runtime-affecting drop is identical.)

findings.title: _match_source silently drops the first user statement when a DataSource body has no recognized source-load line
findings.description: _source_load_boilerplate_end_index scans the cleaned body, skipping leading import lines and source-load statements. If it never sees a source-load statement (saw_source_load stays False) but idx is still in range, the final branch returns `_statement_end_index(cleaned, idx)` instead of `idx`/0. That advances PAST the first non-boilerplate user statement and reports it as boilerplate, so _match_source's start_idx skips it and extract_user_code drops it from the result. The effect is silent corruption of user code: (a) a single-statement no-load source body returns '' (ALL user code lost); (b) a multi-statement body drops the FIRST statement, e.g. `a = 1` / `df = df.with_columns(x=a)` / `return df` extracts only `df = df.with_columns(x=a)`, which now references an undefined `a` (broken code); (c) `import numpy as np` + one transform returns '' (import treated as boilerplate, then the lone transform skipped). This contradicts the function's own contract and the sibling codegen-side helper _strip_source_load_boilerplate_from_code (lines 407-409), which correctly guards `has_source_load = any(...)` and returns the code UNCHANGED when no load is present. _match_external also handles the no-load case correctly (lines 642-645 rewind to first_import_idx). Only the source path regresses. Reachable for hand-authored / legacy / externally-produced DataSource pipeline files parsed via _config_builder.py:251 (_extract_source_user_code); the normal codegen round-trip is unaffected because _gen_data_source always emits `df = read_data_source(...)` which is in _SOURCE_LOAD_PREFIXES.
findings.evidence:
Lines 495-496: `if not saw_source_load and idx < len(cleaned): return _statement_end_index(cleaned, idx)` returns the end-index of the FIRST user statement rather than its start. Probe via .venv python: `_extract_source_user_code('    """d"""
    df = df.with_columns(x=1)
    return df')` -> '' (whole body lost). `_extract_source_user_code(body where lines = a=1 / df=... / return df)` -> 'df = df.with_columns(x=a)' (a=1 dropped). `_source_load_boilerplate_end_index(['a = 1','df = df.with_columns(x=a)','return df'])` -> 1, dropping cleaned[0]. Contrast `_strip_source_load_boilerplate_from_code('df = df.head()
df = df.tail()')` -> 'df = df.head()
df = df.tail()' (preserved). No existing test in tests/test_parser_helpers.py (TestExtractSourceUserCode, all use a scan_parquet/read_data_source load) or tests/test_ast_return_boundaries.py covers the no-load source body.

findings.title: ModelScore/RatingStep boilerplate matchers anchor on the wrong line when the generated-call token appears in a string literal or comment
findings.description: _match_model_score finds the scoring boilerplate by `"score_from_config(" in stripped and not stripped.startswith(("from ", "import "))`. This is a raw substring test over the textual line, so a comment or string literal containing the token before the real call line is matched first. It then walks parentheses from that wrong line and treats the REAL `result = score_from_config(...)` line (and anything between) as user code, which _finalise_model_score then rewrites `result`->`df`, leaking `df = score_from_config(...)` into the saved user code box. _match_rating_step has the identical defect for `apply_rating_step_from_config(`. Unlike the return-boundary detection (which the module docstring deliberately migrated to an AST walk to avoid exactly this class of string/comment confusion), these matchers remain stringly-typed. Severity is low because it requires a user comment/string containing the exact generated-call token positioned before the real call, but the failure is silent and corrupts round-tripped code.
findings.evidence: Probe via .venv python: body with a comment `# call score_from_config(...) below` preceding the real `result = score_from_config(source, config="s.json")` -> _extract_model_score_user_code returns 'df = score_from_config(source, config="s.json")\ndf = df.head()', i.e. the generated scoring line was NOT stripped and was rewritten into user code. Same with a string literal: `note = "uses score_from_config(x)"` preceding the real call -> identical leak. Line 538: `if "score_from_config(" in stripped and not stripped.startswith(("from ", "import "))`. Line 555: `if "apply_rating_step_from_config(" not in stripped: continue` (same substring approach).

findings.title: estimate_safe_training_rows accepts build_node_fn and preamble_ns but never uses them (vestigial probe-era params, wasted caller work)
findings.description: estimate_safe_training_rows declares two parameters - positional build_node_fn (line 835) and keyword preamble_ns (line 838) - that are never referenced anywhere in the function body (842-998). They are leftovers from the old probe-based estimator that the module docstring (lines 13-17) says was replaced by the metadata approach. The metadata path needs neither a node-builder nor a preamble namespace. Confirmed via grep over the whole src tree: the only reads of these names in this module are the parameter declarations themselves. The real caller src/haute/routes/_train_service.py:_estimate_ram goes to genuine effort to supply them - it imports `_build_node_fn` from haute.executor (line 702) and threads `preamble_ns` through purely to pass at lines 715-716 - all of which is discarded. The test suite likewise feeds an elaborate ~20-line dummy fixture `_build_dummy_node_fn` (tests/test_ram_estimate.py:268) into the ignored positional slot in ~25 call sites; every one of those tests would behave identically with None.
findings.evidence: Grep of src/haute/_ram_estimate.py for `build_node_fn|preamble_ns` returns only lines 835 and 838 (the declarations) - no usages in the body. Caller _train_service.py:712-718 passes `_build_node_fn` positionally and `preamble_ns=preamble_ns`; the import `from haute.executor import _build_node_fn` (line 702) exists solely for this discarded argument. Tests pass `_build_dummy_node_fn` (test_ram_estimate.py:268-279) as the ignored 3rd arg throughout (lines 328,353,375,...).
findings.est_reduction: Remove 2 parameters from the public signature; lets _estimate_ram drop the `from haute.executor import _build_node_fn` import and stop threading preamble_ns to this call; lets tests delete the ~20-line _build_dummy_node_fn fixture and ~25 redundant positional args. Net ~30+ LOC across src+tests.
findings.behavior_preservation: Both parameters are read nowhere in estimate_safe_training_rows, so removing them cannot change its output. Existing tests that pass _build_dummy_node_fn/preamble_ns produce identical RamEstimate results today (the values are ignored), so dropping the args is behaviour-preserving. (Public signature change: callers in _train_service.py and modelling.py and the tests would be updated in the same change.)

findings.title: Count-based column fallback subtracts len(excluded) without checking presence, silently under-estimating columns (and thus RAM) when excluded names are not in the resolved schema
findings.description: When _resolve_target_columns_detail returns None but the simpler count walker _resolve_target_columns returned a column count, the ELSE branch at line 928 computes `n_columns = max(n_columns - len(excluded - preserved_excluded_join_keys), 1)`. It subtracts the *cardinality* of the exclude list from the count with no verification that those excluded names actually exist among the counted columns. If `exclude` contains any name absent from that schema (a user typo, or a feature produced by a downstream transform the count walker stopped before reaching, or - per the existing SIMP-4 verdict - the non-string-selected_columns / diamond-revisit cases where detail aborts to None while the count still resolves), the subtraction removes more columns than are really excluded. The result is an undercounted n_columns -> undercounted base_bytes_per_row/peak_bytes (lines 941-953) -> an over-optimistic RAM estimate that can skip a needed downsample and allow an OOM. This is precisely the silent-incorrect-fallback the project's CLAUDE.md warns against. The asymmetry is telling: the IF branch (line 913-921, when detail IS available) filters over the ACTUAL resolved columns (`if column not in excluded`), so absent excluded names are correctly ignored there; only the count-based ELSE branch over-subtracts. Note this is a distinct *correctness* defect, not the SIMP-4 simplification (which only evaluated merging the two walkers and treated the ELSE branch as an intentional weaker fallback without flagging the over-subtraction).
findings.evidence: Line 905-909 builds `excluded` from the target's exclude config; line 928 does `max(n_columns - len(excluded - preserved_excluded_join_keys), 1)`. Contrast the detail path at 916-920 which iterates `for column in target_columns.columns if column not in excluded` (presence-checked). Reachability of the ELSE branch is pinned by tests/test_ram_estimate.py:569-576 (patches _resolve_target_columns->4, _resolve_target_columns_detail->None, asserts probe_columns==2 for exclude=['a','b']); with exclude=['a','zzz'] (zzz absent) the same path would yield probe_columns=2 instead of the correct 3, under-counting by 1. SIMP-4 verdict (review/03-simplification/findings-raw.json:3212) confirms this ELSE branch runs 'precisely when the detail walker yields None' and the int count is load-bearing there.

coverage.notes: Verified-clean / investigated-but-NOT-reported (to avoid noise or overlap with known catalog): (1) Edge-join column resolution (_resolve_edge_join_columns) and its coalesce/suffix handling are CORRECT - empirically confirmed against Polars 1.39.2 that left_on/right_on default coalesce DROPS the right key and on= collision suffixes the right copy, matching the estimator exactly. (2) _source_column_base_widths lines 804-805 (uncompressed_size is None fallback) is NOT dead - unreachable via the read_parquet_metadata production path (every column always keyed) but deliberately reachable and pinned by direct-construction unit tests at test_ram_estimate.py:1257-1298. (3) line 978 peak_per_row=peak_bytes/total_rows has no zero guard but is unreachable when total_rows==0 because peak_bytes is then 0 and the `<= usable_ram` branch returns first. (4) The _resolve_target_columns vs _resolve_target_columns_detail duplication and divergence are already covered by SIMP-4 (verdict 'unsound', do-not-merge); _csv_row_count physical-lines by the known CSV finding + BUG-2; _count_source_rows_for_node/_detailed_source_metadata_for_node dispatch dup by SIMP-6; _detailed_parquet_metadata identity column_width_keys by SIMP-10; available_ram_bytes cgroup-blindness + structure by the known cgroup finding + SIMP-7 - none re-reported. (5) _jsonl_row_count over-counts blank/trailing lines but that is the same physical-line class as the known _csv finding, low value - not separately reported. (6) available_vram_bytes reports only GPU[0] total for multi-GPU - plausibly intentional, low value, not reported.

findings.location: src/haute/trace.py:262-271 (_find_target_row_index) and its use in execute_trace at 489-491
findings.title: _find_target_row_index silently returns the first of multiple matching rows, unlike the hardened ambiguity handling in _correlate_rows_posthoc
findings.description: When execute_trace's positional row-identity check fails (cold trace after the preview cache was evicted and joins reordered rows), it relocates the clicked row via _find_target_row_index(target_df, row_values). That helper intersects row_values with target_df.columns ('shared') and returns the index of the FIRST row whose shared columns all match, with no detection of multiple matches. This is the exact anti-pattern the post-hoc correlation layer was explicitly hardened against: _find_matching_row / _correlate_rows_posthoc record an 'ambiguous_row_match' diagnostic and return None rather than silently selecting a row when >1 candidate matches (see _trace_correlation.py:355-368, 387-397). The relocated row_index is then used as the anchor for all upstream correlation, so an ambiguous relocation silently produces a trace for the wrong row instead of raising the existing 'Trace data does not match the preview row' ValueError or surfacing a diagnostic.
findings.evidence: trace.py:264 `shared = [col for col in row_values if col in df.columns]`; 268-271 loops and `return idx` on the first all-match, no count of further matches. Contrast _trace_correlation.py:357-368 where exact_row_indices with len>1 calls _record_ambiguous_row_match and returns None,-1. execute_trace.py:489-491 `matched_index = _find_target_row_index(...); if matched_index is not None: row_index = matched_index` — accepts the first-match index unconditionally. Realistic trigger is narrow: row_values normally equals the target node's own visible columns, so 'shared' is usually the full row and identical rows yield an identical trace; the conflation requires row_values to carry a key absent from the (changed) target_df AND two rows colliding on the remaining shared columns. Impact is therefore low, but the silent first-match selection is inconsistent with the module's stated 'fail loudly rather than show wrong data' contract.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: Column-origin regex \b{column}\s*= false-matches an equality comparison (column ==) as an assignment
findings.description: In the failed-execution fallback, _prune_to_column_relevance scans each node's raw config code and treats the node as an origin of the traced column when the code contains '.with_columns(' AND re.search(rf'\b{re.escape(column)}\s*=', code) matches. Because the pattern stops at the first '=', it also matches the leading '=' of a comparison operator: a bare `premium == 5`, `premium >=`-no(only '='), specifically `premium ==`/`premium =` both match. A node that merely COMPARES the column (e.g. filters on it) but does not assign it is then added to origin_ids and force-tagged column_relevant=True, broadening the referenced-column ancestor walk. The effect is over-inclusion of steps in the trace, never wrong cell values, so impact is low; and the most common Polars form `pl.col("premium") == 5` does NOT match (the column name is quoted, so the `==` is not directly adjacent to the identifier), which further narrows the trigger to bare-identifier comparisons.
findings.evidence: trace.py:874 `if rc and ".with_columns(" in rc and re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(column)}\s*=", rc):` then 875-876 `origin_ids.add(s.node_id); s.column_relevant = True`. Verified empirically with the project venv: for column='premium', 'premium == 5' -> True (false positive), 'premium=5' -> True, but 'pl.col("premium") == 5' -> False, 'premium != 2' -> False, 'premium >= 1' -> False, 'net_premium = 3' -> False. A stricter pattern (e.g. requiring `=` not followed by `=`, or matching `<col>\s*=\s*` excluding `==`) would eliminate the comparison false-positive.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

coverage.notes: Both NEW findings are low-severity/low-confidence. Verified against the known catalog: SIMP-9 (execute_trace length/extraction + the line-472 KeyError-on-failed-target-with-row_values, which the SIMP-9 verdict explicitly documents as behaviour-to-preserve) is treated as KNOWN and NOT re-reported. The preview-cache-key reconstruction in _materialize_eager_outputs (projected preview_fps[0] reconstructed from row_values keys rarely equals the GUI's stored requested_preview_columns key, and target-only previews are skipped via missing_preview_nodes) was examined and judged a performance-only miss-then-cold-execute path, not a correctness defect (cold execution is correct; reuse only fires when the full ancestor chain is present and read-only). _is_integer_output_column confirmed correct: polars DataType.is_integer is a classmethod (datatypes/classes.py:86/201) so the getattr+callable guard works. _resolve_preview_snapshot reader/dict/None dispatch and TypeError-on-bad-return verified sound. _prepare_graph return-tuple order matches the reuse-branch unpacking. trace_result_to_dict double to_json_safe is idempotent. Empty preview_fps guard in the dict branch is defensive but unreachable from execute_trace.

findings.title: checkpoint() skips memory-pressure-event evaluation when only rss_limit_bytes is set (gate ignores rss_limit_bytes), diverging from the budget check that honours it
findings.description: checkpoint() samples RSS only when `self.memory_limit_bytes is not None or self._active_stage_stack()` (lines 705-709); it does NOT consider `self.rss_limit_bytes`. When the sample is skipped, rss_bytes stays None and `_observe_rss` is not called (lines 710-711) - and `_observe_rss` is the SOLE path to `_record_memory_pressure_events` (line 851). Therefore, for an ExecutionContext that has `rss_limit_bytes` set but `memory_limit_bytes is None` and no active stage on the current thread, a bare `checkpoint()` call evaluates the hard budget (because `_check_memory_budget` re-samples at line 867 and `_effective_rss_limit_bytes()` returns `rss_limit_bytes`) but silently performs NO memory-pressure threshold evaluation. This is an internal inconsistency: `_check_memory_budget`, `_record_memory_pressure_events`, and `_effective_rss_limit_bytes` all treat `rss_limit_bytes` as a valid limit source, but the checkpoint() sampling gate alone does not, so the 50/75/90% advisory pressure events (and their callback/publish side effects) are never produced for such a context at checkpoint boundaries.
findings.evidence: Line 705-709: `rss_bytes = self.memory_sampler() if self.memory_limit_bytes is not None or self._active_stage_stack() else None` - omits `self.rss_limit_bytes`. Line 710-711: `if rss_bytes is not None: self._observe_rss(...)`. `_observe_rss` (835-856) is the only caller of `_record_memory_pressure_events` (851). Meanwhile `_effective_rss_limit_bytes` (950-952) returns `self.rss_limit_bytes` first, so a context with `rss_limit_bytes` set and `memory_limit_bytes=None` HAS an effective limit; `_check_memory_budget` (863-869) re-samples via `self.memory_sampler()` when rss_bytes is None and enforces it - proving the limit is live, yet pressure events are skipped. Reachability: in the shipped codebase admitted contexts (create_admitted_execution_context, _execution_admission.py:455-457) always co-set memory_limit_bytes AND rss_limit_bytes, so checkpoint() samples; the gap is only hit by direct ExecutionContext(rss_limit_bytes=...) construction, which is why this is latent rather than active.

findings.title: ExecutionStageMetric and ExecutionStageSummary duplicate ~16 identical fields with a 20-line manual field-copy in to_summary()
findings.description: ExecutionStageMetric (lines 143-191) and ExecutionStageSummary (lines 194-237) declare the same ~16 fields (name, operation, profile, elapsed_ms, node_id, job_id, rss_start/end/peak_bytes, rows_in/out, bytes_read/written, columns_scanned, n_collects, n_checkpoints, schema_version) differing only in that the summary adds a materialised rss_delta_bytes field (the metric exposes it as a property) and reorders elapsed_ms vs node_id. to_summary() (171-191) then manually re-lists all 17 keyword arguments to copy one into the other. Any field added to the timed metric must be added in three places (metric field, summary field, to_summary copy) or it silently fails to surface in the public trace. The split could be collapsed (e.g. summary derives from the metric via a single helper that injects rss_delta_bytes, or the property is computed in to_dict) to remove the parallel field list and the hand-written copy.
findings.evidence: ExecutionStageMetric fields lines 147-163; ExecutionStageSummary fields lines 198-215 - byte-for-byte the same names/types/defaults except rss_delta_bytes (added at 207) and the elapsed_ms/node_id ordering. to_summary() lines 172-191 passes all 17 fields by hand. The only real transformation is `rss_delta_bytes=self.rss_delta_bytes` (line 181), which the property at 165-169 already computes.
findings.est_reduction: ~25-30 lines (eliminate the duplicated field block and the manual to_summary copy)
findings.behavior_preservation: Refactor-only; the public ExecutionStageSummary.to_dict() shape (including rss_delta_bytes) and all field values must remain byte-identical. Risk is real because the frozen public summary is a stable serialization contract validated by ExecutionMetricsPayload and frontend fixtures, so any merge must keep field order/defaults and the materialised rss_delta_bytes exactly; this is why confidence is low - the split may be an intentional internal-vs-public boundary.

findings.title: get_status.changed_files mangles renamed files into a single 'old -> new' string
findings.description: When a file has been renamed, `git status --porcelain` emits a single line of the form `R  old.py -> new.py` (status code 'R', two-char status + space, then 'old -> new'). The parser does `line[3:].strip().strip('"')`, which yields the literal string `old.py -> new.py` as ONE entry in `changed_files`, instead of the new path `new.py`. Consequently the status panel shows a nonsensical pseudo-filename for every rename, and any consumer treating entries as real paths (e.g. opening the file) breaks. The same line[3:] slice also fails to C-unescape git's quoted paths (git emits `"my file.py"` / backslash-escaped octal for non-ASCII and special chars); `.strip('"')` removes only the outer quotes and leaves embedded escapes intact. Note save_progress/_auto_commit are unaffected because they parse `git diff --cached --name-only`, which prints each path on its own line with no arrow form — only get_status uses the porcelain arrow format.
findings.evidence: Reproduced: `git mv a.py b.py; git status --porcelain` -> `R  a.py -> b.py`. With this single line, the loop appends `('R  a.py -> b.py')[3:]` = `'a.py -> b.py'` (after strip) to changed_files. Expected entry is `b.py`. No test in tests/test_git.py exercises a rename, so this is uncovered.

findings.title: _get_user_slug falls back to os.getlogin(), which raises OSError when stdin is not a TTY (servers/containers)
findings.description: When `git config user.name` is unset/empty, `_get_user_slug` falls back to `os.getlogin()`. `os.getlogin()` reads the controlling terminal and raises `OSError: [Errno 25] Inappropriate ioctl for device` (or similar) in any environment without a controlling TTY — daemonized servers, many Docker containers, systemd services, and some CI runners. Because `_get_user_slug` is called inside `get_status`, `create_branch`, and `list_branches`, an unconfigured git identity in such an environment turns into an UNCAUGHT OSError that escapes the GitError funnel and becomes a generic HTTP 500, rather than a clean, branch-able username. The codebase already has the correct, robust idiom for exactly this in src/haute/deploy/_utils.py:get_user(), which uses `getpass.getuser()` wrapped in `except (KeyError, OSError)`. getpass.getuser() consults LOGNAME/USER/LNAME/USERNAME env vars before falling back, so it works headless; os.getlogin() does not. This helper is inconsistent with that established pattern and is the fragile choice.
findings.evidence: Line 202: `return _slugify(os.getlogin())`. Contrast src/haute/deploy/_utils.py:15-20 `get_user()` -> `try: return getpass.getuser() except (KeyError, OSError): return 'unknown'`, whose tests (tests/test_deploy_utils.py:96-104) explicitly cover `OSError('no tty')` and `KeyError('no user')`. _git has no analogous guard and uses the more failure-prone os.getlogin().

findings.est_reduction: 1 line (the unreachable `else f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{branch}"` arm)
findings.behavior_preservation: exact — str.split never returns an empty list, so the else arm is never taken; removing it (use `parts[-1]` unconditionally) preserves behavior identically.
findings.title: archive_branch has an unreachable `else` fallback on `parts = branch.split('/')`
findings.description: `parts = branch.split('/')` is then used as `archive_name = f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{parts[-1]}" if parts else f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{branch}"`. `str.split('/')` ALWAYS returns a non-empty list (e.g. `'x'.split('/') == ['x']`, `''.split('/') == ['']`), so `if parts` is unconditionally truthy and the `else` arm is dead code. Additionally, `branch` is non-empty here because `_validate_ref_name(branch)` (line 875) rejects empty names, so `parts[-1]` is always a real value. The ternary can be reduced to `archive_name = f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{parts[-1]}"`.
findings.evidence: Line 886-888. `branch.split('/')` cannot yield [] for any str input; `_validate_ref_name` already guarantees branch != ''. Hence the else branch is unreachable.

findings.title: Continuous banding silently overwrites the source float column, destroying NaN/Inf for all downstream nodes
findings.description: In the continuous-banding path, when the banded column is Float32/Float64, _apply_banding rewrites the column with `pl.when(col.is_nan() | col.is_infinite()).then(pl.lit(None)).otherwise(col).alias(column)` and assigns the result back into `lf` (lines 110-116). Because this `alias(column)` targets the SAME column name (not a temporary), the returned frame carries a permanently mutated source column: every NaN and +/-Inf in the input column is replaced by null. The output band column is produced separately, so the mutation is a pure side effect on the input factor. Any downstream node (or the user's post-banding code) that reads the original column afterwards sees null where the data was Inf/NaN, with no log, no warning, and no record that a value was dropped. The docstring frames this as an internal step to make NaN/Inf 'fall cleanly to the default' for the band, but the implementation leaks that nulling into the frame returned to callers. This reaches both the GUI executor (executor re-exports _apply_banding, used by _apply_banding_factors) and the standalone codegen path via apply_banding_from_config. It only matters when output_column != column (when they are equal the final band overwrite makes the intermediate moot). This is the silent-corruption class the project's CLAUDE.md explicitly forbids ('code should be allowed to fail loudly... far superior to a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice').
findings.evidence: Reproduced via public entry point: apply_banding_from_config(pl.DataFrame({'si':[inf,100.0]}).lazy(), {factors:[{banding:'continuous',column:'si',outputColumn:'si_band',rules:[{op1:'>=',val1:0,op2:'<',val2:1e9,assignment:'band'}]}]}).collect()['si'] -> [None, 100.0]; the input Inf is gone. Also via _apply_banding(lf x=[nan,1.0,inf,5.0], 'x','band','continuous',...): result['x'] == [None,1.0,None,5.0] while only result['band'] should have been derived. Code trace: line 116 reassigns `col = pl.col(column)` after the mutating with_columns at 110-115, and nothing restores the original column before `return lf` at 133. No test asserts the source column is preserved after continuous banding of NaN/Inf — existing tests (e.g. test_inf_in_banding_sanitized_to_default) only assert the band output, so the regression is unguarded.

findings.title: Linear chain validation checks full node_map, not the routing-pruned set, so a pruned/non-ancestor parent is silently dropped from wiring
findings.description: build_linear_execution_chain_functions validates base_node_id and chain_node_ids membership against node_map returned by _prepare_graph, raising ValueError('... not in the prepared graph') for anything missing. But _prepare_graph returns prepared.node_map == graph.node_map (the FULL graph: see projection.prepare_graph lines 2116/2130), whereas the actual wiring downstream relies on id_to_name, which contains ONLY the nodes in `order` = topo-sort of `needed` (ancestors of target_node_id that survived live-switch/source pruning; projection.py:2126-2128). The 'missing' check therefore does not match its stated contract: a node that is present in node_map but absent from id_to_name (because it was pruned by prune_live_switch_edges under routing_source='batch', or is simply not an ancestor of target_node_id) passes the check. It is then passed to _build_funcs as a chain parent via chain_parents, and _build_funcs computes src_ids = [pid for pid in parents_of.get(nid, []) if pid in id_to_name] (_execute_lazy.py:1475). Because the parent is filtered out by `if pid in id_to_name`, the first chain node is built with an EMPTY source list and no error is raised — a silently mis-wired chain that produces a wrong frame instead of failing loudly. The sole current caller (_optimiser_service.py:3967) derives base/chain as single-parent ancestors of body.node_id, so it is usually safe, but a source/live-switch-pruned branch under routing_source='batch' can still remove a chain node from id_to_name while leaving it in node_map, making this reachable. The validation should be performed against the routing-scoped set (id_to_name / order), not the full node_map, so a chain node that did not survive routing fails loudly.
