findings.title: Backtick-quoted table names map to a different cache file than their unquoted form (cache-key inconsistency / fragmentation)
findings.description: `_TABLE_NAME_RE` (line 33) explicitly permits optionally backtick-quoted identifiers per part: `^`?[\w-]+`?\.`?[\w-]+`?\.`?[\w-]+`?$`, so both `cat.schema.table` and `` `cat`.`schema`.`table` `` (and partially-quoted mixes) pass validation in `fetch_and_cache` and in the route gates (databricks.py:39, files.py:194). `_cache_path_for`, however, only normalizes `.`, `/` and `\` to underscores (line 163) and leaves backticks intact. As a result the same logical table produces two distinct cache files: `cat_schema_table.parquet` versus `` `cat`_`schema`_`table`.parquet ``. A user who fetches the table using the quoted form and later reads it (or whose stored config later switches quoting) gets a `CacheNotFoundError` / a second redundant fetch instead of a cache hit, and two GUI configs that differ only by backtick-quoting silently maintain separate caches for identical data. The backtick character is a legal filename character on both Windows and POSIX, so this fails silently (no exception) rather than loudly. Note the cache directory itself is consistent (both go through `_cache_path_for`), so the divergence is purely keyed on the exact table string supplied by each call site.
findings.evidence: Regex at line 33 accepts ```cat`.`schema`.`table```. `_cache_path_for` line 163: `safe_name = table.replace(".", "_").replace("/", "_").replace("\\", "_")` — no `.replace("`", ...)`. So `cat.schema.table` -> `cat_schema_table` while ```cat`.`schema`.`table``` -> ```cat`_`schema`_`table```; `result.parent` is still the cache dir so the path-traversal guard (line 166) passes and no error is raised. read_cached_table (line 442) and fetch_and_cache (line 310) both key off the raw `table` string, so a quoted fetch + unquoted read miss each other. Existing tests cover Unicode/homoglyph collisions (test_databricks_io.py:844-887) but never the backtick case.

findings.title: _validate_select_clause rejects legitimate SELECTs whose string/identifier literals contain a denylisted word (e.g. WHERE status = 'DELETE')
findings.description: `_DANGEROUS_SQL_RE` matches the denylisted keywords on bare `\b` word boundaries anywhere in the stripped query, with no awareness of SQL string literals or backtick-quoted identifiers. A perfectly valid, read-only SELECT that merely references one of these words as data is rejected with a `ValueError`. Examples: `SELECT * FROM t WHERE status = 'DELETE'`, `SELECT * FROM t WHERE event = 'UPDATE'`, `SELECT * FROM t WHERE op IN ('CREATE','GRANT')`, or a backtick-quoted column whose name is exactly one of the keywords (`` SELECT `update` FROM t `` — backtick is a non-word char so `\bUPDATE\b` fires). Because the `query` field is GUI-editable free text and string-literal filters are a normal thing for a pricing analyst to write, this is a real usability/correctness limitation: legitimate queries are blocked. It is consistent with the module's fail-loud philosophy (it raises rather than silently mis-handling), and the keyword set is deliberately conservative, so the severity is low — but the matcher's inability to distinguish keywords-as-syntax from keywords-as-data means valid input is refused.
findings.evidence: Line 36-39: pattern is `\b(DROP|DELETE|INSERT|UPDATE|ALTER|TRUNCATE|EXEC|EXECUTE|CREATE|GRANT|REVOKE|UNION|LATERAL)\b` with IGNORECASE, applied via `_DANGEROUS_SQL_RE.search(stripped)` (line 82) over the whole query with no string-literal stripping. `'DELETE'` inside a SQL single-quoted literal still presents `DELETE` flanked by `'` (a non-word char) on both sides, so `\bDELETE\b` matches and line 84 raises `ValueError(f"Query contains forbidden SQL keyword: {match.group()!r}")`. Substring-style names like `update_ts` are correctly NOT matched (trailing `_` keeps the word boundary closed), confirming the matcher only over-blocks the exact-word-as-literal case, which is the realistic failure.

findings.title: _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions is never called (dead code)
findings.description: The function _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions (lines 259-275) builds and returns a tuple of recoverable exception classes, but it is never imported or invoked anywhere in src/ or tests/. The only live consumer of the parse-time fallback logic is the predicate form _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception (line 278), which is called at _config_builder.py:335 inside _validate_user_contract and re-derives the same isinstance check inline. The tuple-builder variant is not in __all__ (which lists only _copy_config_keys, _build_node_config, _attach_code_from_body, _resolve_node_config) and has no callers. It mirrors _execute_lazy._compute_boundary_check_exceptions, which IS used there to build an `except` tuple — but in _config_builder the tuple form was never wired up; only the predicate form is used. It is pure dead code.
findings.evidence: Grep for `_compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions` across the whole repo returns only: (a) its own definition at _config_builder.py:259, and (b) review/metrics JSON files. Zero import sites (the only `from haute._config_builder import ...` statements pull _resolve_node_config, _attach_code_from_body, _build_node_config). Its sibling predicate _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception is the one actually called (line 335). __all__ at lines 39-44 does not export it.
findings.est_reduction: ~17 LOC (the entire function body plus its lazy mlflow import block)
findings.behavior_preservation: Deleting the function removes no behaviour: it has no callers, so no code path changes. The live fallback decision is made solely by _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception at line 335.

findings.title: Parse-time contract fallback swallows ImportError/RuntimeError that the runtime boundary check was deliberately narrowed to re-raise (silent-failure drift)
findings.description: Both _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions (line 268: `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]`) and the live predicate _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception (line 284: `isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError))`) treat ImportError and RuntimeError as recoverable 'fall back to opaque contract' conditions. Their docstrings explicitly claim they mirror the runtime boundary check: line 262-263 says 'Matches ``_execute_lazy._BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS`` — the parse-time fallback must not swallow more than the runtime boundary check would', and line 281-282 says 'Matches ``_execute_lazy``'. That invariant is now VIOLATED. The runtime sibling (_execute_lazy._compute_boundary_check_exceptions / _is_boundary_check_exception) was deliberately narrowed in commit 34aff403 ('Phase 3 audit — narrow 4 exception catches') from `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]` down to `(ConfigError, OSError, MlflowException)`, with a detailed rationale in its docstring (_execute_lazy.py:140-150): RuntimeError ('Persistently corrupt model artifact' from _load_with_bounded_retry) and ImportError (missing catboost/rustystats backend) are real deploy/infra bugs that must surface loudly, NOT be silently downgraded to an opaque contract. The parse-time copy in _config_builder.py was not updated in that commit (34aff403 touched only _execute_lazy.py), so it still carries the old wide set. Consequence: if a node declares `contract=...` and _derive_parse_time_contract raises ImportError or RuntimeError (e.g. a contract function that imports an optional backend, or a corrupt-artifact RuntimeError), _validate_user_contract (line 334-346) catches it and silently treats the builder as fully opaque (Contract.opaque()), so a genuinely drifted/wrong user contract annotation passes parse-time validation unflagged — exactly the silencing the runtime narrowing was meant to prevent. The referenced symbol `_BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS` in the docstring does not even exist (the real names are _compute_boundary_check_exceptions / _is_boundary_check_exception), confirming the docstring drifted from reality.
findings.evidence: git show 34aff403 -- src/haute/_execute_lazy.py shows the line `-    exc_types: list[...] = [ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]` replaced by `+    exc_types: list[...] = [ConfigError, OSError]`, with commit body 'Dropped RuntimeError and ImportError from the tuple. Kept: (ConfigError, OSError, MlflowException)'. `git show 34aff403 --name-only` lists only src/haute/_execute_lazy.py (config_builder untouched). Runtime predicate _execute_lazy.py:171 now reads `if isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError)):` whereas parse-time _config_builder.py:284 still reads `if isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError)):`. The two are no longer in sync despite the docstring asserting they are, and the parse-time set is a strict SUPERSET, so it 'swallows more than the runtime boundary check would' — the exact condition the docstring says must not happen.

findings.title: canonical_json is NON-deterministic for sets/frozensets containing NaN floats — violates the documented order-independence contract for unordered containers
findings.description: canonical_json's contract (module docstring lines 81-99 and _canonicalise docstring lines 119-123) promises that sets/frozensets 'whose elements are the same regardless of the order they were inserted' encode identically because unordered containers are sorted. This is broken when a set/frozenset contains two or more NaN floats. _canonicalise (line 141-143) calls sorted(members, key=_sort_key); _sort_key maps every float (NaN included) to ('2_num', value). Because all NaN comparisons return False, sorted() cannot impose a total order on the NaN members and leaves them in their incoming (hash-/insertion-determined, hence arbitrary) relative positions. Distinct NaN objects also have distinct, effectively-arbitrary hashes, so the set's iteration order — and therefore which slots the surrounding non-NaN elements occupy relative to the NaN run — varies. Result: two logically-equal sets produce DIFFERENT canonical JSON, so two identical configs/policies yield different fingerprints (phantom cache misses), and the digest is unstable across processes/insertion orders. This is silent: sorted() does not raise, so the 'fail loud, never silent' guarantee the surrounding code advertises is bypassed for this case. The property test deliberately excludes NaN (tests/test_caching_correctness.py:504-510 uses allow_nan=False with a comment that NaN breaks equality), confirming the case is unhandled rather than intentionally specified. canonical_json is THE digest encoder (used by _graph_base_fingerprint node configs, runtime_input_extra_keys, and _dataframe_execution_cache execution_policy/payload, the last of which the code comments explicitly note may contain sets).
findings.evidence: Cross-process reproduction (3 separate interpreter runs, each 2000 trials shuffling [nan,nan,nan,1.0,2.0,3.0] before set()): each run produced TWO distinct outputs — '[1.0,2.0,3.0,NaN,NaN,NaN]' and '[1.0,2.0,NaN,3.0,NaN,NaN]'. A 7-element variant produced 4 distinct outputs in one run. Trace: _canonicalise(set) -> members=[..NaN..,1.0,..] -> sorted(members, key=_sort_key); _sort_key(NaN)=('2_num', nan); pairwise key comparisons against nan are all False so Timsort performs no reordering of nan-adjacent elements -> output order == set-iteration order, which is governed by per-object NaN hashes and insertion. By contrast canonical_json([nan,1.0,nan]) is stable across 50 runs (lists preserve order), isolating the defect to the unordered-container (set/frozenset) sort path.

findings.location: src/haute/_cache.py:198-201 (_graph_base_fingerprint node line) and 429-432 (graph_fingerprint extra_keys/context join)
findings.title: Node-line and extra-key fingerprint serializations use unframed pipe/newline joins and are NOT injective — a node id or extra key containing '|' or '\n' collides distinct inputs to one fingerprint
findings.description: _graph_base_fingerprint builds each node line as f"{n.id}|{n.data.nodeType}|{canonical_json(config)}" (line 200) and joins all node+edge lines with "\n".join(parts) (line 218). GraphNode.id is an unvalidated bare str (src/haute/_types.py:605 — no pattern/validator), so an id containing a newline lets ONE node masquerade as the concatenation of TWO different node lines, making two structurally-different graphs hash identically. The same non-injective pattern recurs in graph_fingerprint (line 431): combined = "\n".join([*extra_keys, *context_parts, base]) — an extra_key containing a newline collides with a different extra_keys tuple. The module deliberately framed EDGES with canonical_json arrays specifically to be collision-proof (see the lines 205-217 comment: 'quoting/escaping rules out separator-content collisions'), but the NODE line and the graph_fingerprint join were left in the unframed delimiter form — an internal inconsistency. Consequence: cache cross-contamination — preview/trace/dataframe-execution entries for one graph (or one set of execution params) served as fresh for a genuinely different one. This is DISTINCT from the known duplicate-node-id finding (findings.json:906, which is about node_map collapsing two same-id nodes); here the colliding ids/keys are different strings and the collision is in the digest material itself.
findings.evidence: Reproduced: PipelineGraph with a single node id='a|polars|{}\nb' (POLARS, config {}) yields the SAME _graph_base_fingerprint (75c649bf6c837eaa) as a two-node graph with ids 'a' and 'b' — the crafted id reconstructs both 'a|polars|{}' and 'b|polars|{}' lines after the join. Separately, graph_fingerprint(g, 'k1\nk2') == graph_fingerprint(g, 'k1', 'k2') (both v5:9bc49183309e7af8) because the single newline-bearing key reproduces the two-key join. Reachability: node ids and extra keys (e.g. trace.py:383 passes target_node_id raw as an extra key) originate from raw graph JSON / source, which is not constrained to exclude '|' or newlines; only the pipe-with-newline cross-line case is needed (pipe-only within one line does not collide because the config-JSON boundary differs — verified). Fix is uniform with the existing edge handling: encode the node line as canonical_json([id, str(nodeType), config]) and frame extra keys/context similarly, which also removes the bespoke f-string format (minor simplification).

findings.title: parse_column_path accepts array-crossing column paths (tail containing '[*]'), producing a silent-None leaf instead of loud-failing
findings.description: parse_column_path only checks that column_path starts with the raw table_path string and that the immediate tail begins with a dot. It never inspects the tail for further '[*]' array iterators. A column path that descends through a NESTED array (a deeper iteration depth than the table) is therefore accepted as if it were a flat leaf, in direct violation of the function's documented contract: 'Raises ApiInputSchemaError if the column's path doesn't sit cleanly under the table's iteration depth.' The returned 'leaf' then carries the literal '[*]' substring, and the downstream resolver (_json_shred._resolve_leaf) splits it on '.' and does dict.get('licenses[*]') against keys that are never literally named with '[*]', so the value resolves to None. The malformed config thus yields silently-null column data at shred/cache-build time rather than the structured 422 that validate_v2_schema's whole purpose (the on-the-wire contract, B3) is meant to produce. This is exactly the 'silent failure that's incorrect and hard to notice' the project guidelines warn against. validate_v2_schema calls parse_column_path at line 366 as its only column-path validity gate, so the gap propagates straight through validation.
findings.evidence: parse_column_path: `if not column_path.startswith(table_path): raise`; `tail = column_path[len(table_path):]`; `if not tail: raise`; `if not tail.startswith('.'): raise`; `return tail.removeprefix('.')`. No check rejects '[*]' inside `tail`. Trace: parse_column_path('$[*].drivers[*].licenses[*].id', '$[*].drivers[*]') -> startswith True, tail='.licenses[*].id', starts with '.', returns 'licenses[*].id'. Then _json_shred._resolve_leaf(value, 'licenses[*].id') (src/haute/_json_shred.py:509-534): '.' in leaf -> splits to ['licenses[*]','id'] -> cur = value.get('licenses[*]') which is None (real key is 'licenses', and it is a list, not a scalar) -> column silently None for every row. Contrast parse_table_path (line 210), which DOES enforce every segment ends with '[*]'; parse_column_path enforces the opposite end (a leaf) but forgets to forbid intermediate array iterators. Existing tests (tests/test_v2_codec_and_shred.py:66-82) cover only a clean leaf and an unrelated-prefix rejection; no test exercises a tail containing '[*]'.

findings.title: row_id_column may reference an unselected (non-emitted) column, yielding a silent None row id in the trace UI
findings.description: The row_id_column membership check tests `row_id_column not in seen_col_names`, where seen_col_names is populated from EVERY column's name regardless of its `selected` flag (built in the column loop at lines 351-360 before any selected filtering). But only `selected: True` columns are emitted into the per-port parquet (see _json_shred.shred_to_buffers line 572: `if not col.get('selected'): continue`), so a row_id_column that names an existing-but-unselected column passes validation yet is absent from the materialised frame. The runtime trace consumer reads it with `target_row.get(row_id_column)` (src/haute/trace.py:560), which then silently returns None — the trace UI shows no row identity instead of the configured one, with no error anywhere. The validator's stated job is to loud-fail invariant violations so the cache route can return a structured 422; here a configuration that cannot work as intended is accepted silently. Confidence is medium because the literal docstring wording (line 275: 'it references a column name in the same table') is satisfied — the defect is that the contract is too weak: it should require the referenced column to be a SELECTED/emitted one.
findings.evidence: validate_v2_schema builds seen_col_names from all columns (line 360 `seen_col_names.add(cname)`) with no `selected` gate; the row_id check at line 397 is `if row_id_column not in seen_col_names: raise`. Emission gate is elsewhere: _json_shred.shred_to_buffers line 572 `if not col.get('selected'): continue` and build path line 817 same, so unselected columns never reach a parquet buffer. Consumer: src/haute/trace.py:558-560 `if n.data.nodeType == NodeType.API_INPUT and n.data.config.get('row_id_column'): row_id_column = ...; row_id_value = target_row.get(row_id_column)` -> None when the column was not emitted. Result surfaced at trace.py:602/988 (row_id_column/row_id_value) -> UI shows null identity, no error.

findings.title: Unreachable None/invalid-handle checks inside validate_edge_join_target_handles loop
findings.description: The per-edge loop at lines 132-145 re-checks `target_handle is None` (lines 133-138) and `config_key is None` (lines 140-145), but both branches are provably unreachable given the validation that runs immediately before the loop. By line 132 the function has already established: (a) `len(present_handles) == len(target_handles)` (else it raises at line 117), so NO element of `target_handles` is None; and (b) `set(present_handles) == set(_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY)` i.e. `{'base','join'}` (else it raises at line 125). Because no element was filtered out by the `if handle is not None` comprehension at line 114, `set(present_handles) == set(target_handles)`, so every element of `target_handles` is exactly 'base' or 'join'. Therefore `target_handle is None` (line 133) can never be true, and `_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY.get(target_handle)` (line 139) can never return None (line 140). The only reachable raise in the loop is the genuine role/source mismatch at lines 147-154, which the tests exercise.
findings.evidence: _ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY = {'base': 'baseInput', 'join': 'joinInput'} -> set is {'base','join'}. Line 117 guarantees no None remains; line 125 (`if set(present_handles) != set(_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY): raise`) guarantees every handle ∈ {'base','join'}. The sole caller, resolve_edge_join_role_indices line 96, forwards target_handles unchanged, and the function is not invoked elsewhere (grep over src/ shows only def + that one call). An invalid non-None handle such as ['base','xyz'] is rejected at line 125 before the loop; a None such as ['base', None] is rejected at line 117. Tests test_edge_join_builder_rejects_target_handle_role_mismatch / test_edge_join_codegen_rejects_target_handle_role_mismatch only reach the line-147 mismatch raise.
findings.est_reduction: ~13 lines (drop the `if target_handle is None` and `if config_key is None` blocks; replace `_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY.get(target_handle)` with a direct `[target_handle]` index since membership is guaranteed).
findings.behavior_preservation: Removing the two unreachable branches preserves behavior exactly: no input that reaches the loop can trigger them, and the surviving line-147 comparison plus the pre-loop checks at 107-130 fully cover all validation outcomes. The error messages they raise are duplicated by the earlier line-117/line-125 raises for the equivalent malformed inputs.

findings.title: Top-level `_`-prefix filter in _prepare_config_for_sidecar is fully subsumed by the immediately-following _strip_internal_keys call
findings.description: `_prepare_config_for_sidecar` first builds `filtered = {k: v for k, v in config.items() if k not in _CODE_KEYS and not k.startswith("_")}` (line 135), then on line 136 immediately runs `filtered = _strip_internal_keys(filtered)`. `_strip_internal_keys` already drops every dict key that is a str starting with `_` at the top level (and recursively). So the `and not k.startswith("_")` sub-condition on line 135 is dead: any `_`-prefixed key it would remove is removed again one line later. Only the `k not in _CODE_KEYS` part (dropping `code`, which does not start with `_`) is load-bearing on line 135. The inline comment claims line 135 is "Kept first so α's allowlist sees a smaller candidate set", but removing the redundant `_`-check does not change that: `_strip_internal_keys` on line 136 still runs before the VALID_KEYS allowlist (lines 149-158), so the allowlist sees the identical smaller set either way.
findings.evidence: Line 135: `filtered = {k: v for k, v in config.items() if k not in _CODE_KEYS and not k.startswith("_")}`. Line 136: `filtered = cast(dict[str, Any], _strip_internal_keys(filtered))`. `_strip_internal_keys` (line 71-76) returns `{k: v ... for k,v in obj.items() if not isinstance(k,str) or not k.startswith("_")}` for a dict — i.e. it strips top-level `_`-prefixed string keys. Therefore the `not k.startswith("_")` clause on line 135 removes nothing that line 136 would not also remove.
findings.est_reduction: ~1 clause (simplify line 135 predicate to `k not in _CODE_KEYS`)
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior-identical: the set of keys surviving lines 135-136 is unchanged because line 136 strips the same `_`-prefixed top-level keys; downstream allowlist and compaction see the same dict.

findings.title: `json.JSONDecodeError` is redundant in the except tuple in find_config_by_func_name (it is a subclass of ValueError, already listed)
findings.description: `find_config_by_func_name` wraps the load in `except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError, ValueError) as exc`. `json.JSONDecodeError` is a subclass of `ValueError` (CPython: `class JSONDecodeError(ValueError)`), and `ValueError` is already present in the same tuple, so `json.JSONDecodeError` can never be the catching type independently — it is dead in the handler list. The tuple is equivalent to `(OSError, ValueError)`. This also makes the intent slightly misleading (it reads as if JSON-decode errors are handled by a distinct branch when they are caught by the broad `ValueError`).
findings.evidence: Line 305: `except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError, ValueError) as exc:`. In CPython `json.JSONDecodeError` derives from `ValueError`; since `ValueError` is in the same tuple, listing `json.JSONDecodeError` adds nothing. `_load_json_object` raises plain `ValueError("duplicate JSON key ...")` / `ValueError("Node config JSON must contain an object")` and `json.loads` raises `json.JSONDecodeError`, both of which are caught by the `ValueError` entry; `read_user_text` file errors raise `OSError`.
findings.est_reduction: 1 redundant exception type in the except tuple

findings.title: Large worker results deadlock: parent joins the child before draining the result queue (classic mp.Queue feeder-pipe deadlock)
findings.description: run_isolated_worker fully waits for the child to exit (_wait_for_worker loops on process.join until not process.is_alive()) BEFORE it ever reads the result queue (_read_worker_payload -> result_queue.get). With multiprocessing.Queue, the child's put() hands the serialized object to a background feeder thread that writes it into an OS pipe with a finite buffer (~64 KiB on Linux). If the pickled result exceeds the pipe buffer, the feeder blocks on the pipe write until the parent reads. But the parent never reads during the wait phase; it only join()s. At interpreter shutdown the child blocks in Queue._finalize_join waiting for the feeder, so the child never exits, and the parent's join() never returns. This is the exact deadlock documented in the stdlib ('a process that has put items in a queue will wait before terminating until all the buffered items are fed... if you join such a process you may get a deadlock'). The module never calls cancel_join_thread and never drains the queue before joining, so the pattern is unconditional.
findings.evidence: Order in run_isolated_worker: (1) _wait_for_worker(process, worker_config) at line 211 -> while process.is_alive(): ...; process.join(timeout=wait_seconds) (lines 329-344), parent NEVER calls result_queue.get here. (2) only after the loop returns does line 213 call _read_worker_payload -> result_queue.get(timeout=1.0) (line 309). result_queue = ctx.Queue(maxsize=1) (line 194) with no cancel_join_thread. Child entrypoint does result_queue.put(('ok', function(...))) then returns (lines 270, 266). For a result larger than the pipe buffer the feeder blocks -> child cannot exit -> is_alive() stays True -> with default timeout_seconds=None the parent loops forever in _wait_for_worker. The docstring promises 'return its pickled result' (line 176) with no size bound, so the primitive is defective for large results; existing tests only return tiny dicts (tests/test_worker_isolation.py:25-26), so this is untested.

findings.title: stop_reason() returning 'completed' raises an uncaught ValueError and silently skips cleanup callbacks
findings.description: stop_reason is typed Callable[[], WorkerTerminalReason | None], and 'completed' is a member of WorkerTerminalReason. If a caller's stop_reason returns 'completed', _wait_for_worker first calls _terminate_process(process) (killing the worker) and then constructs IsolatedWorkerStoppedError(terminal_reason='completed'), whose __init__ raises ValueError('completed is not a valid stopped-worker reason'). That ValueError is NOT an IsolatedWorkerError, so the 'except IsolatedWorkerError' arm in run_isolated_worker (line 236) does not catch it. It propagates out through the finally (queue closed) and skips the entire cleanup section (lines 245-251) -> parent-owned cleanup_callbacks never run, contradicting the module contract that 'the parent ... always runs them after the child reaches a terminal state' (lines 178-180). The validation that rejects 'completed' is placed in the exception constructor (after termination) instead of where stop_reason is read, turning a guard into a cleanup-bypassing crash.
findings.evidence: _wait_for_worker lines 331-334: reason = config.stop_reason(); if reason is not None: _terminate_process(process); raise IsolatedWorkerStoppedError(terminal_reason=reason). IsolatedWorkerStoppedError.__init__ lines 116-117: if terminal_reason == 'completed': raise ValueError(...). run_isolated_worker line 236 catches only IsolatedWorkerError; the ValueError bypasses lines 245-251 so _run_cleanup_callbacks is never invoked. WorkerTerminalReason (lines 17-25) includes 'completed', so the offending return value is type-valid.

findings.title: Cleanup-failure details are lost when a primary worker error is also present (only a count is surfaced)
findings.description: When the worker fails (primary_error set) AND one or more cleanup callbacks also fail, run_isolated_worker attaches only str(cleanup_error) as a note to primary_error and then discards cleanup_error. But str(IsolatedWorkerCleanupError) is just 'Isolated worker cleanup failed in N callback(s)' -- it contains neither the underlying exception types nor their messages/tracebacks. The actual cleanup exceptions live in cleanup_error.errors, which is dropped (not chained as __cause__/__context__, not attached to primary_error). So in the common 'worker failed and its temp-dir cleanup also failed' case, the operator sees only a count and cannot tell what cleanup broke. (When primary_error is None the cleanup_error is raised directly and callers can still inspect .errors, so the loss is specific to the dual-failure path.)
findings.evidence: Lines 246-249: if primary_error is not None: if cleanup_error is not None: primary_error.add_note(str(cleanup_error)); raise primary_error. IsolatedWorkerCleanupError.__init__ (lines 139-144) sets the message to f'Isolated worker cleanup failed in {len(errors)} callback(s)' and stores self.errors = tuple(errors); only the message (the count) reaches add_note, and cleanup_error (holding .errors) is never re-raised or chained on this path.

findings.title: Final 'raise IsolatedWorkerCrashedError' after has_result check is unreachable
findings.description: The trailing 'raise IsolatedWorkerCrashedError(...)' at lines 254-257 can never execute. To reach it, control must pass lines 246 (primary_error is None) and 250 (cleanup_error is None) and 252 (has_result is False). But has_result is set True iff status == 'ok' (line 220); every other status raises an IsolatedWorkerError inside the try (status=='error' -> line 226; else-branch -> line 232), which is caught and stored in primary_error. Hence primary_error is None implies status was 'ok' implies has_result is True implies the function already returned at line 253. The same CrashedError is already raised defensively (and pragma-no-cover'd) at lines 231-235 for the impossible non-'ok' status, making lines 254-257 a redundant unreachable duplicate (and, unlike line 231, it is not even pragma-excluded).
findings.evidence: has_result only set True at line 220 under 'if status == "ok"'. 'elif status == "error"' raises at 226; 'else' raises at 232 (both IsolatedWorkerError, caught at 236 -> primary_error). Therefore at line 252 primary_error is None <=> status was 'ok' <=> has_result True <=> returns at 253; lines 254-257 are never reached.
findings.behavior_preservation: Removing lines 254-257 (the unreachable branch) preserves behavior; the live defensive crash path is the pragma-excluded else-branch at 231-235.
findings.est_reduction: 4 lines

findings.title: Unpicklable worker result is misreported as a generic crash (and can be misclassified as memory_limited) instead of a clear pickling error
findings.description: _isolated_worker_entrypoint does result_queue.put(('ok', function(...))). multiprocessing.Queue.put returns immediately; serialization happens later on the feeder thread. If the function's return value is not picklable, the feeder raises PicklingError on the child's feeder thread (printed to the child's stderr) and never delivers the item; the child then exits 0. The parent's _read_worker_payload waits 1.0s, times out (queue.Empty), and raises IsolatedWorkerCrashedError with exitcode=0 and no indication that the real cause was an unpicklable result. Worse, IsolatedWorkerCrashedError feeds exitcode into _exitcode_looks_memory_limited; while a clean exitcode 0 won't trip it, any exit signal coincidence could mislabel this as memory_limited. Net effect: a clear 'result is not picklable' contract violation is surfaced as an opaque crash, costing a fixed 1s delay and hiding the root cause. (Partly an inherent mp.Queue limitation, but the primitive could detect the empty-queue-after-clean-exit case and report it specifically; the 'error' path already proves cross-process delivery of failure detail is feasible.)
findings.evidence: Line 270 put(('ok', function(*args, **kwargs))) with no pre-serialization/picklability check. _read_worker_payload lines 308-314: result_queue.get(timeout=1.0) -> on queue.Empty raises IsolatedWorkerCrashedError(exitcode=exitcode, ...). The error message (line 95) only reports exitcode, never that delivery failed due to pickling. The sibling 'error' branch (lines 271-281) deliberately sends only plain strings precisely so failures are deliverable, showing the asymmetry.

findings.title: Verbatim string factor labels that look like int-like floats are silently corrupted on compact->expand round trip
findings.description: The compact-write side (`_compact_entry_rows` -> `_canonical_sidecar_key` -> `normalise_rating_key`) keeps string factor labels VERBATIM (strings are never collapsed by `normalise_rating_key`). But the expand-read side (`_expand_entries_map.walk` -> `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`) applies a 'legacy float-string migration' that collapses any int-like float-string map key: '25.0'->'25', '1.0'->'1', '1e1'->'10', '5.'->'5'. So a legitimate, non-numeric string label such as a price band '25.0' (or any banding/categorical label that happens to parse as an int-valued float) is silently rewritten after a single save/load cycle. The rating lookup join keys on the exact label, so after `collect_node_configs` (compact write) + `parse_pipeline_source` (expand read) the table entry's key changes and the row STOPS MATCHING -- a silent wrong-result defect, not an error. The `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key` docstring frames this as scoped legacy migration, but it cannot distinguish a legacy float that `str()` wrote as '25.0' from a genuine verbatim string label '25.0', and `normalise_rating_key`'s own docstring explicitly promises 'String keys are deliberately verbatim -- 25.0 is a label, not a number, and never collapses', which the expand path violates.
findings.evidence: Inline trace via .venv python: `_canonical_sidecar_key('25.0')` -> '25.0' (compact write keeps it) but `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key('25.0')` -> '25' (expand read collapses). Full round trip: cfg tables[0].factors=['band'], entries=[{'band':'25.0','value':7.0}] -> compact map {'25.0':7.0} -> expand -> entries=[{'band':'25','value':7.0}] (label changed from '25.0' to '25'). 3-factor variant ({'a':'1.0',...}) likewise yields a='1' after round trip. Values in the leaf position are correctly NOT migrated (only keys), confirming the asymmetry is key-specific. The compact/expand pair is the real save (`_config_io._prepare_config_for_sidecar` line 163) and load (`_config_io._normalise_loaded_config` line 120) path, so this is reachable in production.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar can emit a sidecar that expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar then rejects (write/read asymmetry)
findings.description: Because the compact-write key normaliser (`_canonical_sidecar_key`, line 201) does NOT apply the int-like float-string migration while the expand-read normaliser (`_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`, line 225) DOES, two distinct row-array labels that differ only in float-string formatting (e.g. '5.' and '5', or '25.0' and '25') are written by `_compact_entry_rows`/`_insert_entry_value` as two distinct, non-colliding map keys (no duplicate raised on the write side). When that same compact sidecar is later loaded, `_expand_entries_map.walk` migrates both '5.' and '5' to '5' and raises a collision ValueError. The result is a save operation that SUCCEEDS but produces a JSON sidecar that can never be loaded again -- the pipeline becomes un-parseable until the user hand-edits the file. The two normalisation helpers are contradictory contracts for the same key space.
findings.evidence: Trace: cfg entries=[{'band':'5.','value':1.0},{'band':'5','value':2.0}] -> `compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar` returns {'5.':1.0,'5':2.0} (write OK, _insert_entry_value sees two distinct leaf_keys '5.' and '5'). Feeding that compact map to `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` raises: "ratingStep tables[0].entries factor 'band' compact key '5' collides with existing key '5.' after legacy key migration to '5'". Root cause confirmed inline: _canonical_sidecar_key('5.')='5.' vs _normalise_compact_sidecar_key('5.')='5'.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: Unreachable list-type guard in normalise_rating_tables
findings.description: `normalise_rating_tables` calls `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar(config)` and then re-checks `if tables is None: return []` (308-309) and `if not isinstance(tables, list): raise` (310-311). But `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` already guarantees its returned `tables` is exactly `None` or a `list` (it returns early with `tables=None`, raises if not a list, otherwise assigns `result['tables']=expanded` which is a list). After the `None` case is handled at 308-309, `tables` is provably a list, so the `not isinstance(tables, list)` branch at 310-311 can never execute. It is unreachable defensive code that duplicates a guarantee made one call up.

Therefore post-call `tables in {None, list}`. normalise_rating_tables handles None at 308-309, leaving only `list`, so 310-311 is dead.
findings.est_reduction: 2 lines
findings.behavior_preservation: Removing lines 310-311 preserves behavior: the only inputs that could reach them already raised inside expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar, and the None case is handled at 308-309.

Passing `factors` into `_normalise_entry_rows` (mirroring `_compact_entry_rows`) would remove the duplicate validation and the unused `outputColumn` re-derivation divergence, and align the two row-processing helpers.

Line 154 inside `_normalise_entry_rows`: `factors = _validate_factors(table, table_index)` -- second call on the identical dict. findings.title: Empty-entries early return skips factor validation, silently accepting/serialising invalid factor lists
findings.description: Both `_normalise_entries_for_table` (272-274) and `_compact_table_for_sidecar` (323-326) short-circuit when `entries == []` BEFORE calling `_validate_factors`. As a result a table whose `factors` is structurally invalid -- e.g. `['', '  ']` (blank/whitespace names) or non-string elements -- is accepted without error as long as its entries list is empty, and `_compact_table_for_sidecar` even emits `entries: {}` for it (because the blank-name list is truthy). The same table with one entry would be rejected by `_validate_factors`. This is an inconsistent contract: validity of `factors` should not depend on whether `entries` happens to be empty. The asymmetry can let a malformed table pass save/load unnoticed and only fail later (or differently) once a row is added.
findings.evidence: Trace: cfg tables[0]={'name':'T','factors':['','  '],'outputColumn':'out','entries':[]} -> compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar returns the table with entries={} and the invalid factors ['','  '] untouched (no ValueError). expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar returns entries=[] likewise unvalidated. With a non-empty entries list, _validate_factors (lines 26-29) would raise "factors[0] must be a column name".
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: cache_state_signature_for_graph catches OSError/ValueError but _path_hash raises RuntimeError on unresolvable ~ paths, so the defensive skip is bypassed and the function crashes preview-key computation
findings.description: In cache_state_signature_for_graph the per-node hash is computed defensively: `try: cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path) except (OSError, ValueError): continue`. The intent is to skip any apiInput whose configured path cannot be hashed. But _path_hash calls `Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()`, and pathlib.Path.expanduser() raises **RuntimeError** (not OSError/ValueError) when a leading `~`/`~user` cannot be resolved to a home directory. RuntimeError is not in the except tuple, so it escapes the `continue` and propagates out of cache_state_signature_for_graph. That function is invoked from execution.py:613 while composing the preview/trace cache key for EVERY preview/trace request (`json_cache_signature = cache_state_signature_for_graph(graph)`), so a single apiInput node whose config path is e.g. `~missinguser/data.json` (or `~/data.json` in a deploy with HOME unset and no pwd entry) turns every preview/trace request that includes that graph into an unhandled-exception 500, instead of the node simply being skipped as designed. The node.data.config['path'] value is free-form user input and is read raw at line 193 with no prior expanduser/normalisation on this code path, so the bad path reaches _path_hash unmodified.
findings.evidence: CPython 3.11.13 pathlib source (inspected via the project's .venv): `def expanduser(self): ... homedir = os.path.expanduser(self._parts[0]); if homedir[:1] == '~': raise RuntimeError('Could not determine home directory.')`. _path_hash (line 90): `os.path.normcase(str(Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()))`. cache_state_signature_for_graph (lines 197-200): `try: cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path) except (OSError, ValueError): continue` — RuntimeError not caught. Caller execution.py:613 has no guard either.

findings.location: src/haute/_json_flatten.py:276-290 (no-op trapdoor reads committed/meta.json via _read_cache_meta) + 151-159 (_read_cache_meta raises on corrupt/non-dict meta)
findings.title: A corrupt committed/meta.json makes mirror_cache_to_committed raise at the no-op-trapdoor read, aborting BEFORE the copytree that would overwrite it — so committed/ corruption is self-perpetuating and silently never repaired
findings.description: mirror_cache_to_committed reads the committed-layer meta for its no-op trapdoor at line 277: `committed_meta = _read_cache_meta(committed_dir) if committed_dir.exists() else None`. _read_cache_meta does `orjson.loads(meta_path.read_bytes())` with NO error handling and additionally raises ValueError if the payload is not a dict. So if committed/<hash>/meta.json is truncated/garbled (e.g. a crash during a prior mirror's copytree, or external tampering) the read raises orjson.JSONDecodeError or ValueError at line 277 — which is BEFORE the atomic copytree-and-swap at lines 293-310 that would otherwise replace the whole committed/ directory (including the bad meta) with a fresh, valid working/ snapshot. The repair path is therefore unreachable while committed/ is corrupt. The save caller (_save_pipeline._mirror_api_input_caches, lines 626-633) wraps the call in `except Exception` and only logs `json_cache_mirror_failed`, so save does not crash but committed/ is left corrupt indefinitely: every subsequent save re-raises and re-logs without ever promoting the good working/ snapshot. This is asymmetric with the rest of the cache subsystem, where a garbled/missing meta is treated as 'stale -> rebuild' (e.g. _data_file_matches returns False on a non-dict signature, is_per_port_cache_valid invalidates pre-W2 caches). Note this is distinct from known finding #13 (which is about the missing build lock / bare rename during the copytree); here the failure occurs at the meta read and prevents the copytree from ever running.
findings.evidence: _read_cache_meta (lines 156-158): `payload = orjson.loads(meta_path.read_bytes()); if not isinstance(payload, dict): raise ValueError(...)` — no try/except. mirror line 277 calls it unconditionally when committed_dir exists, before the copytree at line 297. Caller _save_pipeline.py:626-633 swallows the exception and only logs. Contrast _data_file_matches (_json_shred.py:261 `if not isinstance(recorded, dict): return False`) which degrades to 'stale -> rebuild'.

findings.title: cache_state_signature_for_graph hashes the same path three times per apiInput node (one explicit _path_hash + two via _json_cache_dir), each a resolve() syscall plus SHA-256
findings.description: Per apiInput node, cache_state_signature_for_graph computes `cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path)` at line 198, then calls `_json_cache_dir(data_path, _LAYER_WORKING)` (line 201-203) and `_json_cache_dir(data_path, _LAYER_COMMITTED)` (line 204-206). _json_cache_dir internally calls `_path_hash(data_path)` again at line 98. So _path_hash — which does `Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()` (a filesystem syscall) plus a SHA-256 over the canonical path — runs 3 times for the same path on every preview/trace cache-key build, for every apiInput in the graph. The already-computed cache_hash could be reused to build both layer directory paths directly (e.g. `Path.cwd()/_CACHE_DIR/<layer>/f'json_{cache_hash}'`), collapsing 3 hashes to 1. Behaviour is identical because _json_cache_dir's hash is the same cache_hash value; only the redundant resolve() syscalls and hash recomputation are removed.
findings.evidence: Line 198 `cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path)`; lines 201-206 each call `_json_cache_dir(data_path, ...)`; _json_cache_dir line 98 `... f"json_{_path_hash(data_path)}"`. Three _path_hash invocations, each invoking Path.resolve() + hashlib.sha256, for one data_path.
findings.est_reduction: ~2 resolve() syscalls + 2 SHA-256 computations per apiInput per preview key (no LOC change required, or a few lines reorganised)
findings.behavior_preservation: Identical output: the layer directory hash equals the already-computed cache_hash; only redundant recomputation is eliminated.

findings.title: Negative `ttl` is not validated and silently turns the cache into a permanent always-miss
findings.description: The constructor validates `max_size >= 1` and `max_bytes >= 1` and the byte/size_of cross-dependencies, but performs NO lower-bound validation on `ttl`. A negative `ttl` (e.g. `LRUCache(ttl=-5)`) is accepted silently. Because `time.monotonic()` is non-decreasing, for any stored entry the expiry check in `get` is `(_time.monotonic() - stored_at) > self._ttl`, and `elapsed >= 0 > negative_ttl` is always True. Every `get` therefore takes the expiry branch, calls `_remove_key`, and returns `None` — so `put` keeps inserting entries that the very next `get` immediately evicts. The cache becomes a no-op that never serves a hit, with no error raised. This is exactly the silent-failure class the project's CLAUDE.md warns against ('code should be allowed to fail loudly'), and it diverges from an existing codebase convention: `src/haute/routes/_job_store.py:76-79` rejects `ttl_seconds < 0` with `ValueError("ttl_seconds must be >= 0")`. The fix is a one-line guard mirroring the other params, e.g. `if ttl is not None and ttl < 0: raise ValueError(f"ttl must be >= 0, got {ttl}")`.
findings.evidence: Lines 93-100 validate max_size and max_bytes but never reference `ttl`. Line 101-102 stores it unchecked: `self._ttl = ttl`. get() lines 127-131: `if self._ttl is not None: stored_at = self._timestamps.get(key, 0.0); if (_time.monotonic() - stored_at) > self._ttl: self._remove_key(key); return None`. For ttl=-5 and any entry stored at t0, at any later get the elapsed `>=0` satisfies `>-5`, so the entry is always removed and None returned. Contrast _job_store.py:76 `if ttl_seconds < 0: raise ValueError("ttl_seconds must be >= 0")`. No test in tests/test_lru_cache.py or tests/test_lru_cache_contracts.py exercises a negative ttl (TestTTLEdgeCases only covers ttl=0).

The module is correct and idiomatic: publish() uses a correct snapshot-under-lock/iterate-outside-lock pattern with per-handler Exception (not BaseException) isolation; _unsubscribe is idempotent and pops emptied event-type keys; RLock guards all registry mutation/reads; snapshot/restore are consistent. The only real defect (GraphUpdatePayload under-declares the graph_fingerprint key the watcher publishes) is already in 'known' and is correctly scoped as a static/type-check contract issue (wire path is correct at runtime because _ws_graph_update_subscriber forwards the full payload via _ws_message_frame). Adjacent angles considered and rejected as non-reportable: ParseErrorPayload exactly matches its {error, source_file} producer (no under-declaration); the snapshot/restore empty-list asymmetry is defensive-only and never triggers because _unsubscribe never leaves empty-list keys; handlers.remove() using == equality is a theoretical edge only for handlers with custom __eq__ (handlers are functions/bound-methods with identity equality here) -- a style nitpick, not a defect; the 'Deep copy' wording in _snapshot_handlers_for_testing is a minor doc imprecision (it is a shallow list copy) but moot since handler references are immutable. The heavy module docstring (~130 lines) is intentional design rationale, not over-complexity. No new bugs or simplifications warranted.

findings.title: Chained and keyword-form pipeline.submodel(...) calls are silently dropped, discarding entire submodels
findings.description: extract_submodel_calls only recognises the single, positional, non-chained form `pipeline.submodel("path")`. It requires the call's `func.value` to be a bare `ast.Name` equal to "pipeline" and reads only `call.args[0]`. Two valid, runtime-supported spellings are therefore silently ignored, returning an empty path list so every referenced submodel (and all of its nodes and edges) vanishes from the parsed graph with no warning: (1) the documented chained form `pipeline.submodel("a.py").submodel("b.py")`, and (2) the keyword form `pipeline.submodel(file="a.py")`. Chaining is explicitly documented in the runtime (`Pipeline.submodel` returns `self`, docstring at src/haute/pipeline.py:477 says "Can be chained: pipeline.submodel(\"a.py\").submodel(\"b.py\")") and is exercised by tests/test_pipeline.py:786 and :792. The sibling helper _extract_connect_calls (src/haute/_ast_helpers.py:336-381) walks method chains down to the base receiver and accepts positional-or-keyword source/target; extract_submodel_calls does neither, so the two paths disagree. Codegen always emits one `pipeline.submodel(\"...\")` per line (codegen.py:1241) so GUI round-trips are unaffected, but any hand-authored pipeline file that uses the documented chaining (or the keyword) syntax silently loses its submodels. This is a silent contract violation that drops graph content rather than failing loudly, contrary to the project's fail-loud policy.
findings.evidence: Confirmed by execution: `extract_submodel_calls(ast.parse('pipeline.submodel("modules/a.py").submodel("modules/b.py")'))` returns `[]`; `extract_submodel_calls(ast.parse('pipeline.submodel(file="modules/a.py")'))` returns `[]`; while the one-per-line form returns `['modules/a.py','modules/b.py']`. Code trace: for the chained expression the outer Call's `func.value` is itself a Call (the inner `.submodel("a.py")`), so `isinstance(func.value, ast.Name)` at line 52 is False and the whole expression is skipped (lines 49-54). For the keyword form `call.args` is empty so the `if call.args and isinstance(call.args[0], ast.Constant)` guard at line 55 is False. Runtime support: src/haute/pipeline.py:470-480 `def submodel(self, file: str) -> Pipeline: ...; return self`; tests/test_pipeline.py:786 asserts `p.submodel('a.py').submodel('b.py')` yields `submodel_files == ['a.py','b.py']`.

findings.title: Direct edge between children of two different submodels loses its boundary handle: dropped on flatten, breaks codegen on re-save
findings.description: When the main pipeline file directly connects an OUTPUT child node of one submodel to an INPUT child node of another submodel (e.g. `pipeline.connect("a_out", "b_in")` where a_out is a child of submodel A and b_in is a child of submodel B), merge_submodels produces a corrupt boundary edge. The cross-boundary edge is first reconstructed as `a_out -> b_in` (lines 143-168), then rewire_edges is applied once per submodel in sequence (line 194). Submodel A's pass sees src_inside → rebuilds the edge as `submodel__A -> b_in` with sourceHandle='out__a_out'. Submodel B's pass then sees tgt_inside and rebuilds a FRESH GraphEdge with target=submodel__B and targetHandle='in__b_in' but does NOT copy the existing sourceHandle, so the result is `submodel__A -> submodel__B` with targetHandle='in__b_in' and sourceHandle=None. Two downstream failures result, neither caught at parse time: (a) flatten=True path — flatten_graph (src/haute/_flatten.py:63-78) only rewrites the source side when sourceHandle is truthy; with sourceHandle=None the source stays 'submodel__A', the edge still references a submodel node at line 77, and the edge is dropped entirely, so the executor runs with the a_out→b_in data dependency silently removed (wrong execution order / missing data flow). (b) flatten=False (GUI/hierarchical) path — codegen later requires every edge whose source is a submodel placeholder to carry an 'out__<child>' sourceHandle and raises ParseError otherwise (codegen.py:1050-1057), so saving the parsed pipeline throws and the round-trip is broken. validate_pipeline_graph_shape_contracts does not detect it: _iter_submodel_child_contexts (src/haute/_graph_shape.py:115-118) computes `_boundary_child_id(None, prefix='out__')` → None and silently skips, so parse appears to succeed. Reachable directly from parse_pipeline_source: explicit pipeline.connect() pairs are passed verbatim as parent_edges to _merge_submodels.
findings.evidence: Confirmed by execution against the real code. flatten=False: merge_submodels with two single-child submodels A={a_out}, B={b_in} and parent_edges=[('a_out','b_in')] yields exactly one edge `submodel__A -> submodel__B sh=None th=in__b_in` (out__a_out handle lost), with submodels['A']['outputPorts']==['a_out'] and submodels['B']['inputPorts']==['b_in'] (so classify_ports correctly identified both ports, but the edge handle was dropped). flatten=True: the same input produces `graph_flattened ... edge_count=0` — zero edges; nodes ['a_out','b_in'] are present but the a_out→b_in dependency is gone. Trace of the loss: _submodel_graph.rewire_edges lines 116-125 (target-side rewrite) constructs GraphEdge(source=e.source, target=sm_node_id, targetHandle=f'in__{e.target}') with no sourceHandle argument, discarding the 'out__a_out' set by A's earlier source-side pass at lines 126-135.

findings.title: normalise_banding_factors silently returns [] for malformed non-list factors instead of failing loudly
findings.description: normalise_banding_factors guards with `if not isinstance(factors, list): return []`. For a malformed config where `factors` is a non-list, non-None value (e.g. a dict, string, or number), this silently returns an empty list, so banding produces zero factors and the node becomes a silent no-op with no error. This diverges from the two sibling functions in the same module — expand_banding_config_from_sidecar (line 80-81) and compact_banding_config_for_sidecar (line 198-199) — which both explicitly `raise ValueError("banding factors must be a list")` for exactly the same malformed input. It also contradicts the project's stated principle (CLAUDE.md: 'code should be allowed to fail loudly... a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice' is to be avoided). There is no upstream schema validation forcing `factors` to be a list (src/haute/_config_validation.py has no `factors` check; src/haute/_builders.py::_banding_columns also uses the lenient `config.get('factors') or []`). The runtime callers (src/haute/_rating.py:225, src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:1807, src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py:506) therefore silently drop all banding for a corrupted/non-list factors blob rather than surfacing the corruption.
findings.evidence: normalise_banding_factors: `factors = config.get('factors'); if not isinstance(factors, list): return []`. Compare expand_banding_config_from_sidecar: `factors = result.get('factors'); if factors is None: return result; if not isinstance(factors, list): raise ValueError('banding factors must be a list')`. Same input class (non-list, non-None) -> one returns [] silently, the other raises. A `None` factors is correctly an empty no-op in both; only the non-list-non-None case diverges.

findings.title: upstream_node_ids docstring 'nearest parents first' is false for DAGs/diamonds
findings.description: The docstring states the result is ordered 'nearest parents first', but the algorithm is a pre-order DFS (pop from the front of `stack` while prepending each node's parents to the front via `stack[0:0] = ...`), not a breadth-/distance-ordered traversal. In any diamond/DAG topology a more-distant ancestor can be emitted before a nearer direct parent. Trace: parents_of = {D:[B,C], B:[A], C:[A]}; upstream_node_ids(D) yields [B, A, C] — A (distance 2 from D) is emitted before C (a direct parent, distance 1), violating 'nearest parents first'. The returned set of ancestors is correct and complete (no node is missed or duplicated), and every current caller is order-insensitive — they either wrap the result in set() (execution.py:489, _dataframe_execution_cache.py:218, _optimiser_service.py:583) or feed it to merge_categorical_level_declarations, which keys results by column and is order-independent (modelling/_feature_contract.py:389, raises on any conflict regardless of declaration order). So there is no current functional impact; the defect is purely a false documented contract that could mislead a future caller who relies on the stated ordering.
findings.evidence: Loop: `stack = list(parents_of.get(node_id, []))`; `current = stack.pop(0)`; `stack[0:0] = parents_of.get(current, [])` — this is DFS pre-order, not nearest-first BFS. Concrete counterexample parents_of={D:[B,C],B:[A],C:[A]} produces [B,A,C], placing grandparent A before direct parent C.

findings.title: Wildcard trusted-host patterns are matched case-sensitively against a force-lowercased host, so any mixed-case '*.' pattern (e.g. HAUTE_TRUSTED_HOSTS=*.Internal.Corp) rejects every host
findings.description: LocalTrustedHostMiddleware normalises (lowercases) exact-match patterns and the incoming Host header, but deliberately leaves wildcard patterns un-normalised. The two sides of the wildcard comparison therefore disagree on case, so a wildcard pattern containing any uppercase letter can never match a real host. Exact patterns are case-insensitive while wildcard patterns are case-sensitive against an always-lowercased host -- an internal inconsistency that silently denies service to legitimately-configured hosts (fail-closed, not a security hole, but a contract bug).
findings.evidence: In __init__ (line 119-122): `self._normalised_allowed_hosts = [pattern if "*" in pattern else _normalise_host_value(pattern) for pattern in self.allowed_hosts]` -> a wildcard like `*.Internal.Corp` is stored verbatim; an exact `Example.com` becomes `example.com`. In __call__ (line 129): `host = _normalise_host_value(Headers(...).get("host",""))` always lowercases the host. The wildcard branch (line 131): `(pattern.startswith("*.") and host.endswith(pattern[1:]))` evaluates `"foo.internal.corp".endswith(".Internal.Corp")` -> False. Contrast starlette's reference TrustedHostMiddleware (.venv/.../trustedhost.py:40,44) which compares both sides raw (consistently case-sensitive); Haute added lowercasing only on the exact-match and host sides. HAUTE_TRUSTED_HOSTS is a documented user knob (_local_security.py:26, server.py:360-363) and the `*.` branch exists specifically to serve it.

findings.title: Positional-only and keyword-only @pipeline node parameters are silently dropped (only ast.arguments.args is read), losing implicit edges and corrupting user-code/config extraction
findings.description: _extract_decorated_nodes builds param_names from `stmt.args.args` only. Python's ast.arguments splits parameters into posonlyargs (before `/`), args (positional-or-keyword), kwonlyargs (after `*`), vararg, and kwarg. Reading just `args` means a pipeline node written as `def node(a, /, b, *, claims_aggregate):` exposes only `b`. Every parameter that names an upstream node but lives in the posonly/kwonly buckets is invisible: its implicit param-name edge is never created by _build_edges, its input-extraction line is not recognised as boilerplate by extract_user_code (mis-extracting the saved code), and for LIVE_SWITCH/CONSTANT-style nodes it is missing from config['inputs']. No error is raised -- a silent contract violation in the same family as the known async-def and submodel-edge drops, but distinct from them and not covered by any known finding. (Machine-generated codegen never emits `/` or `*`, so this only bites hand-edited pipelines, but those are an explicitly supported edit surface.)
findings.evidence: src/haute/_graph_builders.py:73 `param_names = [arg.arg for arg in stmt.args.args]` -- a project-wide grep shows `posonlyargs`/`kwonlyargs` are referenced nowhere in src/haute, so these parameter kinds are never recovered on the healthy AST path. Downstream: _build_edges (line 143-154) derives implicit edges from `node_info['param_names']`; _config_builder._build_node_config sets `config['inputs'] = param_names` for LIVE_SWITCH (line 108) and passes param_names into _extract_user_code/_extract_rating_step_user_code/etc (lines 180,183,203,218,223,249-255), which use them to strip the codegen input-extraction lines. n_params=len(param_names) (line 74) is likewise undercounted. Example: `@pipeline.polars` over `def transform(claims, *, adjustments): ...` where `adjustments` is another node -> the (adjustments, transform) edge is dropped and the `adjustments = inputs[...]` boilerplate line is treated as user code.

findings.title: Implicit param-name edges are not de-duplicated among themselves, so a duplicated parameter name (reachable via the regex fallback) yields two GraphEdges with an identical id
findings.description: The implicit-edge loop dedups each candidate only against the explicit_edges set; it never guards against producing the same implicit edge twice. If a node's param_names contains the same name twice and that name matches an upstream node, two GraphEdge objects with the identical id `e_{src}_{tgt}` are appended. The healthy AST path cannot produce duplicate params (Python rejects `def f(a, a)` at parse time), but the regex fallback path (_parser_regex._find_function_blocks) builds param_names by naively splitting the parameter text on commas with no de-duplication, and that path runs precisely on malformed source. The result is a duplicate React Flow edge key and a parent listed twice in build_parents_of. The explicit-edge branch already prevents its own duplicates via explicit_edges; the implicit branch lacks the symmetric guard.
findings.evidence: src/haute/_graph_builders.py:143-154 iterates `for param in node_info['param_names']` and appends an edge with `id=f"e_{pair[0]}_{pair[1]}"` whenever `pair not in explicit_edges`, with no seen-set across implicit edges. src/haute/_parser_regex.py:532-539 builds param_names via `for p in params_text.split(','): ... param_names.append(name)` (no de-dup). A regex-fallback node `def f(source, source)` with an upstream node `source` would emit two `e_source_f` edges. Low likelihood (requires already-broken source) but a concrete asymmetry with the explicit-edge de-dup.

findings.title: Local-origin check compares the raw origin host string against a fixed set, so a non-canonical IPv6 loopback origin (e.g. http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]) is rejected
findings.description: _is_local_origin tests `origin_host in _LOCAL_ORIGIN_HOSTS` where the set is the literal `{'localhost','127.0.0.1','::1'}`. _normalise_host_value returns the bracket-stripped inner address verbatim (lowercased) without canonicalising it through ipaddress, so the fully-expanded loopback form `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` does not equal the compressed literal `::1` and the origin is treated as non-local (403). The comparison is naive string equality rather than an ip_address-normalised compare. Fails closed (rejects a valid loopback), so it is a robustness/correctness gap rather than a bypass; browsers almost always emit the compressed `[::1]` form, which is why this is low-impact.
findings.evidence: src/haute/_local_security.py:32 `_LOCAL_ORIGIN_HOSTS = {'localhost','127.0.0.1','::1'}`; line 64-82 _normalise_host_value returns `host[1:closing]` (the inner address, never canonicalised); line 147 `return origin_host in _LOCAL_ORIGIN_HOSTS or origin_host in _configured_origin_hosts()`. Origin `http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]:5173` -> origin_host `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` != `::1` -> not local. _is_ipv6_literal already exists and ip_address(...).compressed would canonicalise both sides.

findings.title: rewire_edges silently drops the external endpoint's port handle on cross-boundary edges, corrupting multi-port wiring
findings.description: When rewire_edges replaces a cross-boundary edge, it correctly synthesises the SUBMODEL-side boundary handle (in__<child> / out__<child>) but throws away the handle on the *external* side of the edge. In the External->internal branch it builds GraphEdge(source=e.source, target=sm_node_id, targetHandle=f'in__{e.target}') with no sourceHandle=e.sourceHandle, so an external multi-output source node feeding a submodel child loses its output-port selector. Symmetrically, the Internal->external branch sets sourceHandle=f'out__{e.source}' but omits targetHandle=e.targetHandle, dropping the external target's input-port role. The module's sibling reconstruction code in _parser_submodels.py:159-167 deliberately preserves these handles (sourceHandle=source_port, targetHandle=target_port) precisely so that 'later rewiring replaces true submodel boundary handles with in__/out__ markers' (comment at _parser_submodels.py:139-142) -- i.e. only the boundary side should be replaced, not the far side. The flatten round-trip (_flatten.py) only restores the target side, and ONLY for edge-join roles via build_edge_join_boundary_target_roles (_flatten.py:30-33, 74); there is NO recovery path for a dropped source-side handle (when a submodel is the SOURCE, _flatten.py:67 sets new_sh=None unconditionally). Consequently a graph that wires an external multi-output node (e.g. a model node emitting frequency/severity frames, or a multi-port apiInput) into a node inside a newly-created submodel ends up, after flatten-for-execution, with an edge from that multi-port node carrying sourceHandle=None, which _execute_lazy.py:103-108 rejects with ValueError 'Edge from multi-port node X has no sourceHandle'. Worse, in the hierarchical (flatten=False) saved graph the wiring intent is silently lost with no error at all. Both callers are affected: routes/_submodel_ops.py:90 passes real GraphEdge objects (cross_edges) straight from graph.edges with handles intact, and _parser_submodels.py:194 passes parent_edge_list whose cross edges carry the preserved source_port/target_port.
findings.evidence: _submodel_graph.py:117-125 (External->internal) constructs the rewired GraphEdge with only targetHandle set; e.sourceHandle is never forwarded. _submodel_graph.py:127-135 (Internal->external) sets only sourceHandle; e.targetHandle is never forwarded. Contrast _parser_submodels.py:159-167 which builds the pre-rewire cross edge WITH sourceHandle=source_port and targetHandle=target_port, and the comment at 139-142 stating only the boundary handle should be replaced. _flatten.py:60-74 recovers a target-side handle only through edge_join_boundary_target_roles (join roles) and sets new_sh=None for submodel-source edges (line 67) -- no source-side handle recovery exists. _execute_lazy.py:103-108 raises ValueError when a multi-port source edge has sourceHandle is None. The existing tests (tests/test_submodel_graph.py:177-285) construct edges via a helper that never sets any handle, so this loss is entirely unguarded.

findings.title: Contract dataclass, _freeze, and _freeze_mapping are duplicated near-verbatim in _builders.py instead of imported from _contracts.py
findings.description: src/haute/_builders.py defines its own Contract dataclass (with opaque/from_tuple/to_tuple/from_user_declared), _freeze, and _freeze_mapping that are functionally identical to the ones in the in-scope src/haute/_contracts.py (confirmed: _builders.py contains no `from haute._contracts import` for these symbols; it redeclares Contract at line 162 and the two helpers at 274/296). The bodies match line-for-line including the redundant first disjunct in _freeze (`isinstance(value,(set,list,tuple)) or (isinstance(value,Iterable) and not isinstance(value,(str,bytes)))`, where the first clause is fully subsumed by the second). _contracts.py was created expressly as the lightweight import surface (module docstring: 'parser/codegen callers need the contract dataclass ... without paying for the full executor-side builder module import'). That goal is exactly served by having _builders.py re-export Contract/_freeze/_freeze_mapping from _contracts.py rather than maintaining a second copy. The duplication is a real maintenance hazard: the two classes are distinct types, so a behavioural change to one (e.g. a new accepted user-declared form, or tightening _freeze) silently diverges, and Contract.from_user_declared's `isinstance(value, Contract)` fast-path (line 67) does not even fire for the other module's Contract (it falls through to the hasattr duck-typing branch). Note this is NOT the known SIMP-7 (which concerns _optimiser_io.py cache-info logging) nor the known codegen _format_contract_kwarg item.
findings.evidence: _builders.py:162 `class Contract:` with opaque@182, from_tuple@187, to_tuple@203, from_user_declared@209; _freeze@274; _freeze_mapping@296 -- bodies identical to _contracts.py:36/44/49/56/63 and 111/133. `grep -n _contracts src/haute/_builders.py` returns only comment/string hits (lines 157, 344), proving no import of these symbols. The redundant set/list/tuple disjunct appears identically at _contracts.py:117 and _builders.py:280.
findings.est_reduction: ~110 duplicated lines removed from _builders.py (Contract + _freeze + _freeze_mapping) by importing from _contracts.py; the deliberate lightweight-import boundary is preserved because _contracts.py imports nothing heavy.
findings.behavior_preservation: Re-exporting from _contracts.py yields one canonical Contract type. Behaviour is preserved for every caller; the only observable change is that the two previously-distinct Contract classes collapse into one, which removes the latent isinstance-fast-path divergence rather than introducing risk. test_column_contracts (which asserts callable identity per _builders.py:344) and the codegen/projection contract round-trip tests should be run to confirm.

coverage.notes: _optimiser_io.py (all 4 funcs): the cache_info misses-vs-hits asymmetry, the missing else-branch in load_mlflow_optimiser_artifact, and the hand-rolled concurrency-fragile hit/miss detector are ALL already covered by the known SIMP-7 (review/03-simplification/findings-raw.json:944-948) -- not re-reported. _contracts.to_tuple intentionally omits inputs_by_parent (tuple form has no fan-in slot; callers use inputs_by_parent directly) -- not a bug. classify_ports correctly does order-preserving dedup and intentionally ignores the source-port tuple element (documented). build_submodel_placeholder is correct. The rewire_edges multi-port handle-loss bug is distinct from the known parser implicit-edge-dropped finding and the known codegen inputs_by_parent cross-boundary mis-attribution finding (new-bugs.md:28), which operate at different layers.

All 20 in-scope functions across src/haute/_logging.py, src/haute/_file_ops.py, src/haute/_path_resolution.py, and src/haute/_graph_shape.py examined in full. Probed many edge cases, each confirmed correct/intentional and test-covered: (1) resolve_runtime_file_path final 'resolves outside the project root' error at line 133 is only reachable under enforce_project_root=True (when False, _candidate_if_allowed never returns None so deduped is always non-empty), so the message is accurate; covered by test_absolute_raw_path_outside_root_is_rejected_when_enforced and pipeline-fallback tests. Validating the whole child graph when submodel__X is in scope is correct. All four in-scope files reviewed in full against their callers and test suites. _config_validation.py: VALID_KEYS is built from flat (non-inheriting) total=False TypedDicts so __annotations__ is complete; NodeType.SUBMODEL_PORT is intentionally excluded (no TypedDict) and that omission is relied upon by _config_io._prepare_config_for_sidecar; warn_unrecognized_config_keys never raises and the underscore-prefix skip is consistent with the write-side allowlist. _topo.py: topo_sort_ids correctly registers isolated nodes and drops unknown-endpoint edges; _find_cycle_nodes (Kahn peel) provably returns a non-empty set whenever graphlib raises CycleError (no empty-error mismatch), correctly excludes acyclic tails and includes cycle-downstream nodes per its docstring; ancestors honours the all_ids filter; the insertion-order tie-break contract is satisfied by every caller (pipeline.py, trace.py, codegen.py, projection.py pass ordered lists). discovery.py: configured-vs-glob dedup uses .resolve() correctly (verified by symlink tests); tomllib import is safe under requires-python>=3.11; configured path join cannot widen the glob scan; the line-97 comment ('when no configured file matched') is mildly imprecise versus the tested accumulate-all behaviour but the behaviour is correct and pinned by test_configured_pipeline_listed_first, so not reportable. _mlflow_utils.py: resolve_version int-sorts versions (MLflow versions are always integer strings on both Workspace and UC registries); search_versions single-quote escaping matches pinned tests; resolve_mlflow_source validates required args per source_type and the global set_tracking_uri pattern is the established, concurrency-tested approach. findings.title: export_trace reports a source column's `origin` as the most-DOWNSTREAM carrier (usually the target node), not its true upstream origin
findings.description:
In the `sources` section, the per-column origin is computed by iterating ALL steps and keeping the LAST step whose `output_values` contains the column:

    origin_node = None
    for s in steps:
        if col in s.output_values:
            origin_node = s.node_name
    sources.append({"column": col, ..., "origin": origin_node})

`output_values` is the FULL output row of each node (every column present at that node's output, including columns merely carried through), not just newly-added columns — confirmed at trace.py:833 `output_values=output_row` where `output_row` is the whole correlated row. Consequently `col` is present in the `output_values` of every step from the column's creation point all the way through to the traced target step. Because the loop overwrites `origin_node` on each match and does NOT break, it returns the LAST (most-downstream) step that still carries the column — which is the target node itself (or the final step), i.e. the OPPOSITE of an origin. The field is named `origin`, the module docstring describes `sources` as 'input columns and their origins', and the test `test_export_includes_input_sources` (test_trace_hero_tdd.py:796) documents the intent as 'Lists each input column and its origin node'. So the value returned is silently semantically wrong. A correct implementation would select the FIRST producing step (e.g. the first step where `col in s.schema_diff.columns_added`, or simply `break` on the first `output_values` match for upstream-most carrier).
